title: Amateur prospector finds $150,000 gold nugget in outback
text:
Sounds of excitement fill the air as an amateur prospector digs his hands into red, rocky dirt.

What he comes up with is something he hopes isn't "a painted rock", but instead a gold nugget worth about $150,000.

He had been digging for several days on Mount Stuart station near Tibooburra, in the north-western corner of New South Wales.

But he said the discovery was one of persistence, after having nearly walked past the nugget.

Loading...

'The machine was squealing'

The lucky prospector, who wishes to remain anonymous, has been fossicking for years and is familiar with coming up empty.

"You dig lots of rubbish … lots of lead bullets, old timer's nails, horseshoes, everything," he said.

Metal scraps are the most common find for prospectors. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

He was finishing up a day of searching in mid-October, when he stumbled across a signal with his metal detector, the Gold Monster 2000.

"It wasn't a loud signal for the size of the piece that it is [but] once I got down to 100 [millimetres] or something like that, the machine was squealing," the prospector said.

"It might have been on the first or second scrape I just seen this bright yellow dot in the centre of the hole."

A lucky Broken Hill prospector has dug up a gold nugget worth around $150,000. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

The gold nugget specked with quartz weighs over 1,200 grams, with testing showing around 940 grams is pure gold.

On spot price, it is worth between $150,000 to $160,000.

But with plans to sell the nugget to a collector, the price could be pushed as high as $200,000, according to the prospector, who has nicknamed his precious find the "Tibooburra Spud".

Prospecting a popular pastime

In his 20-odd years selling prospecting supplies in Broken Hill, Greg Spangler has only seen one other person find a gold nugget which weighs over a kilogram.

It is more typical to find gold flakes or smaller nuggets weighing only a few ounces.

"We have a fictitious club [called] the Ounce Club … but not many people [are] in the 'Kilo Club'," Mr Spangler said.

Greg Spangler from Broken Hill Prospecting Supplies says more people are taking up prospecting as a hobby. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

Despite the rarity of discovering a nugget worth six figures, Mr Spangler believes a surge in gold prices has drawn more people to the hobby.

"It's got a lot of people interested," Mr Spangler said.

Gold prices soared to new heights this year, peaking in January at almost $8,000 per troy ounce (or 31.1 grams). While the price has since dropped, it's still sitting favourably at about $5,700 per troy ounce.

The nugget has been affectionately named the "Tibooburra Spud" by the prospector who found it. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

Beyond the chance of an instant boost to your retirement fund, Mr Spangler said there were other benefits to the hobby, including exercise, fresh air and a bit of quiet.

"You get up in the morning, you're the first one to see the sunrise … it's very peaceful," he said.

"Just another pastime you can involve the whole family in."

More gold in Tibooburra

Gold prospecting around Tibooburra, which dates back to the late 1880s, is a major drawcard for many tourists.

Today, fossicking on the Tibooburra Common, an area surrounding the remote township, is currently banned while Native Title permissions are being pursued.

But at least two stations in the region, Mount Stuart and Gumvale, allow fossicking for a fee.

The lucky prospector found his $150,000 nugget with the Gold Monster 2000. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

And Mr Spangler said for anyone looking to have a go, there could be plenty more gold to be found.

"[It could] keep going forever and ever, because every time it rains, other people find gold where they didn't before," he said.

As for the prospector, he has just one tip for would-be fossickers: "Just keep walking, keep swinging [and] keep digging every target."

title: Three-game Bledisloe Cup series looms as new deal struck
text:
The Wallabies are set to play two Bledisloe Cup Tests at the MCG in a matter of years, fuelling hopes that one of rugby union's biggest rivalries could be permanently returning to a three-game series.

Rugby Australia struck a multi-year deal with the Victorian government which secures Melbourne to host the Wallabies and New Zealand in the Rugby Championship in 2027 and an additional Bledisloe Cup Test in 2029.

It comes as Lang Park in Brisbane is set to stage the first Anzac Day Bledisloe Cup Test next April, which sets up a three-match series between the bitter rivals for the first time since 2021.

Wallabies outclassed by All Blacks The Wallabies fall to the All Blacks for the 13th straight time, as their trans-Tasman rivals record a convincing 43-21 win in Sydney.

Whether a three-game series would persist beyond next year has been a hot question exercising pundits.

But Monday's announcement of an additional Test in Melbourne in 2029 will very much boost optimism that a permanent three-game Bledisloe Cup series could return.

That is because Brisbane has also secured the rights for the 2029 Anzac Day Test along with the 2031 instalment.

RA officials were coy on whether the announcement was a signal for a return to full-time three-Test series, and were unsure if 2028 would be similar to 2027 considering no Anzac Day Test has been announced.

An extra Bledisloe Cup Test would favour the Wallabies, who haven't held the trophy since 2002 and have been unable to win both Tests since it became a two-game duel in 2022.

In 2026, they were utterly humiliated by the All Blacks, conceding a mammoth 93 points across the two games, which dealt coach Les Kiss a harsh reality check ahead of next year's home Rugby World Cup.

Wallabies admit they 'faced the music' It was brutal and confronting, but the Wallabies knew they had to face the reality of Saturday night's defeat to the All Blacks sooner rather than later.

Regardless of the three-Test speculation, having a Bledisloe Cup Test at the MCG next July is set to be a stellar moment for the sport in Australia as it ramps up preparations for the World Cup.

The Wallabies last played the All Blacks at the MCG in 2023, where a crowd of 83,944 filled the historic ground, which was the largest rugby attendance in more than 20 years at the time.

Last year, 90,307 watched the Australians' second Test against the British & Irish Lions, breaking the Lions' all-time crowd record.

"The Melbourne Cricket Ground is one of the world's great stadiums — and a jewel in Australia's sporting crown — and the Wallabies are proud to be hosting the All Blacks at the iconic venue in 2027," RA chief executive Phil Waugh said.

"The Wallabies and All Blacks have played only four previous Test matches at the MCG, and this Bledisloe Cup encounter will mark 30 years since both teams took to the hallowed turf for the first time.

"The Wallabies and All Blacks have won two Tests apiece at the 'G and another enthralling contest awaits next year."

Australia will also meet the All Blacks at least one more time in 2027 when they face off in their second Pool A match of the Rugby World Cup at Sydney's Olympic stadium.

AAP

title: RLWC quick hits: Big crowds and bigger scorelines in week two
text:
The second week of the Rugby League World Cup was short on genuine contests as the tournament's haves and have-nots collided.

Aside from Australia's win over Fiji, where the gallant Bati gave the Kangaroos a hell of a scare, it was big scorelines across the board.

But with fans across three Australian states and two other counties voting with their feet, there are still plenty of quick hits from the second round of matches.

1. Tongan wall holds yet again

Tonga took care of business in their win over Lebanon. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

For the second week in a row, Tonga's opponent enjoyed plenty of field position and for the second week in a row Tonga's scrambling defence proved more than up to the challenge.

After holding England to 12 points last week, despite the English enjoying 34 tackles inside the red zone to Tonga's 18, they repeated the dose against Lebanon on Friday night.

Tonga down Lebanon in World Cup Tonga's win over Lebanon kicked off what's expected to be a lopsided weekend in the Rugby League World Cup but there's still something to be gained amid the blow-outs.

The Cedars came in with an offload-heavy game plan and had some success moving the ball up the field. By the end, they had 29 tackles inside the attacking 20 to Tonga's 30, but that was where they stalled.

Some of it was due to a lack of creativity but there were plenty of last-gasp Tongan efforts to deny Lebanese players who looked tryline bound, and it means Tonga carry a strong form line into Sunday's blockbuster against Samoa.

2. Samoa running riot over PNG is a sign of the times

Rarely will you see two halves of a single game more different than what Samoa and Papua New Guinea dished up in Port Moresby.

The Kumuls held the gloves up well through the opening 40, trailing just 14-6 at the break and could have been even closer had Robert Derby successfully grounded the ball for their second try.

But what followed was a procession: Samoa scored 50 unanswered points in the second half, as their size and athleticism totally overwhelmed PNG, who had just four sets in the entire stanza.

Of all the blowout results this weekend, this more than any other was a sign of the times. Rugby league's embrace of the set restart rule and the increased speed of the game makes it almost impossible for an underdog team to stay in the fight beyond a certain point and when things break they can break badly.

Samoa only had to make 36 tackles through the entire second and the Kumuls only got over halfway for two tackles.

They finished the game conceding six tries in 15 minutes against a side they had held their own against for the whole first half.

There were plenty of less-extreme examples of the same through this year's NRL season, most notably when a top eight side conceded the third-most points in a game ever, but it's been turned up to greater levels through this World Cup given the talent and fitness disparity and it stacks the deck even further against the underdogs.

3. France's woes continue in England smash-up

England ran out easy winners against a hapless France outfit. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre )

England beat the clock against their old rivals in Perth, running out 82-0 winners in a result that means France have conceded 160 points in as many minutes through their two matches.

It's hard to find any silver lining for Les Chanticleers and ahead of their tournament finale against Lebanon, the French game finds itself in a strange position.

The potential for growth or a return to the glory days when France were one of Test football's true powers is always the dream, and with two Super League clubs in Catalans Dragons and Toulouse — giving France more professional teams than New Zealand — they seemingly have the ingredients and infrastructure for improvement.

France just cannot seem to close the gap on their more illustrious rivals. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

All but two of this year's squad were home-grown players and since 2020 they have won nine of the 16 Tests they have played, with all seven losses coming against England or Samoa.

Problem is, across those seven games they have been outscored by a cumulative total of 394-44, with this England loss the worst of them.

There's greater pathways to the top for French talent than ever before but they can't seem to close the gap between them and the big dogs.

If anything, the gap has become wider. Nine years ago, in the 2017 World Cup, they played England at the same ground and lost 36-6 a week after losing to Australia 52-6.

Those scorelines aren't exactly a good time, but they're not a point-a-minute for two straight weeks either.

The Southern Hemisphere racing ahead of the north is a wider issue for the sport, but France are the collateral damage and they don't have a contingent of heritage NRL players to paper over the cracks.

4. Christchurch puts its best foot forward

Despite the result, it was a healthy crowd in Christchurch. (Getty Images: Kai Schwoerer)

Despite Esom Ioka's first-half hat-trick that briefly gave the Cook Islands the lead, few would have ever expected the Aitu to trouble New Zealand for long in their match at Te Kaha in Christchurch.

That didn't stop a sell-out crowd of 26,800 coming through the gates, marking the fifth biggest Test attendance of the past century in New Zealand and the highest ever for a game outside of Auckland.

It was a strong week of crowds throughout the tournament — Tonga and Lebanon pulled in more than 25,000 and Australia topped 40,000 for the second week in a row despite taking on Fiji.

But with the NRL expansion race heating up as the league prepares to hand out a licence for a 20th team, Christchurch showing up in droves did their chances of winning the bid no harm at all.

5. Fiji take Australia to the brink

Australia are through to the semi-finals of the World Cup after their win over Fiji. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris )

Speaking of that Australian-Fiji crowd, the 41,108 punters who packed into Lang Park didn't just push the attendance past that of the 2017 World Cup final at the same venue, they were treated to easily the best clash of the weekend.

On the back of an inspired display by five-eighth Kurt Donoghoe and a hat-trick to Castleford winger Semi Valemei, Fiji pushed Australia all the way before a late Jacob Preston try wrapped up a 36-22 win for the green and golds.

Consider the previous margins between the two (42-8, 54-6 and 64-0 in their last three meetings) and it's a measure of how far the Bati have come and how this World Cup is more up for grabs than one might think.

A couple of contentious calls and some killer instinct in key moments got the Kangaroos home.

But on what they've shown through two weeks, Samoa, Tonga and New Zealand will all fancy their chances of springing an upset should they meet Australia, who have wrapped up a semi-final berth in surprisingly shaky fashion.

title: Law must change on aged care algorithm to allow human override, ombudsman says
text:
The Commonwealth Ombudsman Iain Anderson has issued a damning report on the aged care algorithm, saying the government should amend the law to allow senior assessors to override its decisions when it gets it wrong.

In a scathing report of more than 100 pages, the ombudsman says the actions of the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, in its administration of the assessment scheme and the algorithm, "have been unreasonable".

The report says the department put the classification algorithm in place "without any meaningful risk assessment, evaluation or analysis, despite the obvious risks that would arise with deterministic automated decision-making".

The classification algorithm was launched on November 1 last year as part of the government's "once in a generation" reforms to aged care and is used to assign people a level of funding to stay at home with support rather than go into a nursing home.

But it has been mired in controversy since its introduction, with hundreds of people appealing its decisions, a more than five fold increase on appeals in the previous year.

In his report released today, Mr Anderson said: "A reasonable person would, in my view, lack confidence that the system is in fact fair and consistent."

In a response to the draft report, the department said it "does not accept this characterisation" that it didn't test the algorithm or validate it.

However, as revealed by Four Corners and by the ombudsman, tests were conducted on an original version of the algorithm created by a consultancy. The algorithm in place today was modified by the department and there was no external validation.

Audit recommended

Mr Anderson also recommends the Australian National Audit Office consider doing an audit of the implementation of the Single Assessment System and the Independent Assessment tool, which is the questionnaire which drives the algorithm, "and in doing so, assesses whether the Department's use of public resources was efficient, economical and ethical".

Analysis: Aged care algorithm leaves people in limbo If the government wants a true indication of the level of feeling in the community, perhaps it should read the thousands of comments on Facebook where discussions about the algorithm, long waitlists, and people dying are growing by the day.

The ombudsman made a total of 10 recommendations, with six being accepted by the government. The first two recommendations, that legislation be introduced to allow override by a human and amending the aged care rules, have not been accepted by the department, and have only been noted.

However, the department has accepted the recommendation for a comprehensive review of the Aged Care Act in relation to the assessment process and algorithm to "identify legal defects, inconsistencies, ambiguities or unintended consequences" and address these issues in a timely way.

It has also accepted the recommendation that any amendment to the act be "preceded by and informed by meaningful consultation with the public".

Department 'incorrectly advising' assessors

Mr Anderson said the department had been wrongly telling assessors that the algorithm outcomes could be changed right up until the new legislation took effect.

This is despite the fact that there was no mechanism in the act or the rules to change outcomes.

"The Department did not, and may still not, understand key components of the legal framework it created, nor did it understand what legal framework it was meant to create," Mr Anderson said.

The government has resisted calls to give blanket permission for delegates for assessment agencies to override the classification algorithm.

It instead passed legislation last week to allow an "escalation pathway" for appeals in exceptional circumstances.

In return for the Coalition's support in passing the legislation, it has commissioned a review into the assessment system and algorithm, with a report due in the first half of next year.

In a statement, Minister for Health and Ageing, Mark Butler, and Minister for Aged Care, Sam Rae, said: "The Government will consider the Ombudsman's report carefully as we continue to improve our aged care system, including the assessments system."

"We're already acting on many of the recommendations to ensure our aged care system is transparent and reliable, and we'll examine what further action we can take to give every Australian confidence in the system."

Over a million people, or 85 per cent of those using aged care, receive services through the home support system.

title: Australia's second largest veggie company admits 'cartel conduct'
text:
Australia's second-largest fresh produce supplier, Perfection Fresh Australia, has admitted to "cartel conduct" by fixing the price of broccoli, cauliflower and iceberg lettuce sold to Aldi stores in New South Wales.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) began civil action in the Federal Court in September 2025 against four vegetable-growing companies, and three individuals, including Perfection Fresh.

The group was accused of working together to illegally fix the price of fresh produce sold at Aldi stores in NSW, Victoria and Queensland between 2018 and 2024.

The ACCC accused four vegetable suppliers of fixing the price of fresh produce. (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

The ACCC said Perfection Fresh had admitted to engaging in cartel conduct on 11 occasions between 2019 and 2020.

Perfection Fresh has agreed to pay a $12 million penalty, subject to Federal Court approval at a later date.

The case against the remaining suppliers — Hydro Produce, Veli Velisha Fresh Produce and Velisha National Farms, and M Fragapane & Sons — is continuing.

Luke Woodward says cartel behaviour can increase prices and harm consumers. (Supplied: ACCC)

In a statement, ACCC Commissioner Luke Woodward said cartel conduct "undermines competition".

"[It] can increase prices, harming consumers and raising the cost of doing business," he said.

"Enforcing cartel laws and protecting competition in the supply of fresh food are ongoing priorities for the ACCC."

Perfection Fresh Australia, which is based in NSW, supplies a broad range of produce including cauliflower, broccoli, iceberg lettuce, Brussels spouts, broccolini and celery to all states and territories.

The company admitted to price fixing on 11 occasions, but the court can penalise only 10 instances: nine contraventions and one attempted contravention.

The other falls outside the period in which a penalty can apply.

A Perfection Fresh Australia spokesperson said the company took full responsibility for its actions.

"We deeply regret any impact it may have had on our relationships and are working hard to rebuild trust with our stakeholders," the spokesperson said.

"We have fully cooperated with the ACCC since becoming aware of the issue and have taken significant steps to strengthen our leadership, governance and compliance systems."

title: Zempilas echoes 'The Road Not Taken' as WA Liberals face difficult choice
text:
In many ways, the work of a politician is the work of a salesman.

And that sales pitch begins at party state conferences, where leaders sell their vision to their most faithful followers.

It's always filled with a necessary helping of optimism, which WA Liberal leader Basil Zempilas obligingly delivered yesterday.

Zempilas was full of hope as he spoke to the WA Liberal faithful. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"There is a pathway to victory in 2029," he said of the next state election.

" It may be a path which takes us down a political road less travelled. "

It's a turn of phrase sometimes linked to 'The Road Not Taken' by American writer Robert Frost which recalls an indecisive traveller facing two diverging paths.

There could hardly be a more apt image of where the WA Liberals are, two and a half years from the next state election.

Tackling the One Nation threat

The party is facing a difficult choice.

Is their best chance of winning back government leveraging the growing levels of support for One Nation?

WA Liberal MPs were all ears as they listened to Zempilas's conference address. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Or does the once-minor party present such an existential threat that it needs to be confronted head-on?

Having laid out everything you'd expect him to — how terrible Labor is doing, how well the Liberals have done at highlighting that, and announcing reforms to payroll tax — Zempilas reaffirmed his view.

"We are not working in partnership with One Nation," he told reporters.

Zempilas spruiked his party's payroll tax policy to reporters before answering questions about One Nation. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"But there is some common ground, and that common ground centres around they want Labor out, and so do we."

In his view: "Any person in my position would be derelict in their duty if they are not considering everything that is before them."

It's a position in stark contrast with others in his party, including Queensland Premier David Crisafulli who yesterday ruled out future negotiations with One Nation.

Challenge laid bare

In times gone by, the current political landscape would have been fertile ground for an opposition to sow the seeds of discontent needed to turf Labor out.

Cost-of-living pressures continue to bite, despite the state's huge surpluses. The health system is struggling to cope with an aging population. A crisis in child protection has dominated headlines for months.

Do you know more? Contact Keane Bourke on encrypted email. Please note you will need your own encrypted email account, such as Protonmail, to ensure end-to-end encryption.

All wicked problems without quick fixes and, perhaps most importantly, contributed to by both major parties.

It was a sentiment reflected on by One Nation's first MP in WA's lower house, Luke Herdegen, as he gave his maiden speech last week.

One Nation MP Luke Herdegen delivered a blunt message in his maiden speech to state parliament. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"I do not feel lonely, because I know my friends are coming," he said.

"It is too late for you to stop it, but I can try to help you understand it.

"The fact is you got complacent. Some of you turned your back on the tides, and some of you simply never knew they were there."

Herdegen told MPs he would soon be joined by more One Nation "friends" in parliament. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

And there was an even more explicit nod to the anti-establishment mentality which seems to be pushing support to One Nation.

"The people do not care about your titles, they do not care about Question Time, the standing orders [rules of parliament] or which of you have booked the members' dining room for 6pm," Herdegen said.

" They care about whether they can afford to put dinner on the table for their families at 6pm. "

Liberals set out stall

Those clear concerns of voters are why federal Liberal leader Angus Taylor spent Saturday morning telling the state conference about his plans to "axe Labor's toxic taxes, waste and red tape".

"We'll make life easier for Australians and Australian businesses, and that means more businesses, more farms, more factories, more infrastructure," he said.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor addressed the Liberal state conference on Saturday. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Meanwhile, federal firebrand Michaelia Cash promised a coalition government would, on its first day, legislate that "a man is a man, a woman is a woman".

Taylor said he was "always happy to stand in front of three flags, as long as they are all Australian flags".

Taylor told the conference crowd about his plans to "axe Labor's toxic taxes, waste and red tape". (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

It was not a matter of one taking priority over the other, Senator Dean Smith clarified the following day, but that a coalition government "will be doing a lot of things on its first day".

Prospect of triple coalition

If that day comes for Taylor, or Zempilas, though, the path they use to get there could drastically change what that first day, and those which follow, looks like.

Zempilas says the Liberals "will consider anything that needs to be considered" in due course. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

But the more complicated path — which would result in a Liberal-National-One Nation government — isn't one which the WA leader said he had considered.

"Our ambition is to govern in our own right, together with our partners from the Nationals, and we will consider anything that needs to be considered at such time as it needs to be," he said.

WA Liberal members offer applause for Zempilas and his speech. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Zempilas himself has acknowledged "there are lots of things that I have seen and heard from One Nation that I wouldn't say or be involved in".

Just imagine how vigorous that debate could get if a close working relationship brought the trio into power.

Don't look back in wonder

Frost's poem concludes: "I took the one [path] less travelled by, and that has made all the difference."

Many have offered their own interpretations of his writing in the century since, including that the traveller's choice never really mattered.

More than two years out from the state election, the WA Liberals are charting their course. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

And yet the poem persists in the minds of some as a call to choose the harder, less popular route, in pursuit of success.

Perhaps that's why Zempilas told his party: "With so much at stake, this is not, friends, a time to be timid. It is a time to be bold."

Zempilas used his speech to declare there was "a pathway to victory in 2029" for the Liberals. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Much like Frosts's writing, the meaning of that call changes in the eye of the beholder.

But by the next state election in 2029, a choice will have to be made.

The party will be hoping it isn't left looking back, wondering about 'The Road Not Taken'.

title: Melbourne Market board quits over appointment of former Demons chief Paul Guerra
text:
The full board of the Melbourne Market Authority (MMA) has quit over the appointment of former Melbourne Football Club chief executive Paul Guerra as boss.

Mr Guerra was chosen by the Victorian government to be the new chair of the statutory authority, which oversees the Victorian government-owned Epping-based fruit and vegetable wholesale market.

Angie Bradbury had been acting chair since May this year, and told the ABC she applied to be appointed to the three-year chair role after serving on the board since 2022.

She has now resigned from the board after being overlooked for the top job.

"I was not prepared to step aside and go back to the board table when I have been an effective leader," Ms Bradbury said.

"This is not about Paul Guerra, I don't understand how the decision has been made, the value it offers and what issue it is [the government] think they are solving," she said.

Ms Bradbury, along with other board members Margaret Burdeu and former Victorian Farmers Federation president Emma Germano, resigned effective October 29.

Acting chief executive and executive director Keith Louie has given his one month notice of resignation.

A letter from two board members prior to the announcement, seen by the ABC, asked Victorian Agriculture Minister Michaela Settle to reconsider the decision.

In the letter, the two board members threatened to resign unless Ms Bradbury was appointed as chair instead.

"We are unwilling to lend our professional standing, governance experience and statutory accountability to an appointment that we consider presents foreseeable and unacceptable risks to the Authority," the letter said.

Ms Settle confirmed the resignations and said Mr Guerra "knows what it takes to lead a major market from his time chairing Queen Victoria Market."

She said she looked forward to seeing Mr Guerra lead Melbourne Market into its next chapter.

Market future hinges on Victorian election

Mr Guerra was removed as the Melbourne Football Club chief in April, seven months into his term, and has begun proceedings against the club in the Federal Court for breach of contract.

The first case management hearing for his case will be heard in court on October 30, the same day he is due to start the three-year term as market authority chairman.

Mr Guerra has been contacted for comment.

The market authority is the statutory authority responsible for overseeing the Melbourne Market at Epping, Australia's largest wholesale fruit, vegetable and flower market.

Last week the Victorian Coalition pledged to sell the Melbourne Market if it won next month's state election, while Labor said it would stay in government hands if Labor won.

Mr Guerra was previously the chief executive of the Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, and of the Royal Agricultural Society of Victoria.

He also was the executive chair of the Queen Victoria Market.

The Victorian government statement regarding his appointment said Mr Guerra brought "significant commercial, governance and stakeholder engagement experience to the role".

Melbourne's wholesale fruit, vegetable and flower market is in Epping. (ABC News: Cath McAloon)

"The Melbourne Market is a significant part of Victoria's fresh produce industry, and I am committed to supporting the market and its users in my role as chair of the Melbourne Market Authority,'" Mr Guerra said in the government statement.

Victorian opposition spokesman James Newbury said the government had undermined merit-based board appointments.

"Victoria’s public boards belong to the Victorian people, not the Labor Party’s mates," he said.

A Victorian government spokesperson declined to comment on Mr Guerra's salary, but said renumeration for such a role ranged from $21,941 to $61,750.

There has also been instability at the executive level of the authority.

Rob Clayton, who was appointed as chief executive of the market authority in March, quit after three months.

He had been appointed after former head of the organisation Mark Maskiell stepped down after almost 14 years.

Matt Elliott will take up the role of chief executive in January. Mr Louie is the acting chief executive.

Jason Cooper from Fresh State, which represents market traders, said the resignations raised "serious questions about the stability and effectiveness of the current governance arrangements," and was disappointed the appointment occurred less than two weeks before Victoria entered caretaker mode.

"Fresh State would be prepared to work with the Victorian government to establish an interim, industry-led governance arrangement until the market’s long-term ownership is determined," he said.

title: Antonelli is two points away from the F1 title, and can win it next week
text:
With his ninth grand prix win of the season on Monday morning (AEDT), Italian Kimi Antonelli put himself on the cusp of winning his maiden Formula 1 drivers' championship.

The 20-year-old Mercedes pilot has been a class above the rest in 2026, and could have sealed the championship with his victory in Texas on Monday, but other results meant he had to wait at least one more week before popping the champagne.

Next weekend's Mexican Grand Prix shapes up to be the coronation of Antonelli as an F1 champion. Here is how he can seal the world title.

Antonelli needs just two more points

Heading into Monday's United States Grand Prix, there were still five drivers who could mathematically catch Kimi Antonelli in the race for the title.

Kimi Antonelli is in just his second season of Formula 1. (Getty Images: LAT Images/Simon Galloway)

But Antonelli's win reduced his challengers to teammate George Russell and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton.

Drivers' championship standings

1: 365 — Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes

2: 242 — George Russell, Mercedes (-123)

3: 241 — Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari (-124)

With just five grands prix left to run, there is a maximum of 125 points a driver can achieve by winning every race.

Antonelli has 365 points, 123 ahead of Russell and 124 over Hamilton.

The maximum total Russell and Hamilton can end the season with is 367 and 366 points, respectively.

That means Antonelli needs to win just one more point to eliminate Hamilton from the title race, and two points to eliminate Russell.

Antonelli can achieve that in Mexico City by finishing ninth or higher.

He would also win the title if neither Russell or Hamilton win the race.

Even if Russell or Hamilton finish exactly 100 points adrift of Antonelli at the end of the race in Mexico, with 100 points still available, the Italian would be crowned champion, as his nine grand prix wins cannot be topped by either rival.

'Very excited' Antonelli wants to win in style

Antonelli has held the lead of the drivers' championship since his victory at the Japanese Grand Prix in round three.

Despite leading since March, Antonelli has dismissed any and all notions of thinking about winning the drivers' championship in just his second season.

But with the championship all but won, he has finally been able to acknowledge that only the most calamitous set of circumstances would deny him becoming champion.

Speaking after his tremendous win in Texas, Antonelli said his mindset for the rest of the 2026 season was to continue pushing and scoring as many points as possible.

"I am very excited. We would love to clinch the title in style with a great result," Antonelli said about his impending title win.

"That's always the mindset, and that is going to be the mindset from now until the end of the season.

"Just going to try and enjoy every moment, because these we'll always remember."

title: 'Meant to be in Perth': Passengers confused by Sydney's new airport
text:
Sydney's new status as a two-airport city is already causing confusion for some travellers.

Julie Lundmark, from Sweden, headed to Melbourne for the weekend from Sydney Airport but was surprised to discover her return flight landed at the brand new Western Sydney International Airport (WSI).

The airport, which has been decades in the making, began operating passenger flights on Sunday.

Ms Lundmark and her friend were on Jetstar flight JQ373 when they realised the mistake.

"We landed here and looked out of the window and had no idea where we were," she said.

"And we looked down the map and we thought to ourselves, we are a little bit lost."

The first international flight departed this morning. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

She said she had checked the name of the airport on her boarding pass a few days ago.

"The funny thing is we googled because we didn't recognise the name 'west airport' that was on the boarding pass, and we googled it and it took us to the normal Sydney airport."

Ms Lundmark said they were left looking for ways to get back to Sydney Airport.

"We have our car parked at the other airport," she told 702 ABC Sydney.

"We are stuck in Western Sydney."

A metro service from St Marys to WSI was not completed before the airport opened, with buses and a free shuttle operating to and from the station being the main public transport options until the rail link opens.

However, Ms Lundmark said given it would take her two hours to get to Sydney Airport, she hoped a friend with a car would help out.

"We've made some panic calls to the city and hopefully someone will pick us up," she said.

"Double check, everyone, on your tickets before."

'I'm meant to be in Perth'

Ms Lundmark was not the only confused traveller at WSI this morning.

One holiday-maker found out he booked a ticket to the wrong airport. (ABC News)

One man who disembarked flight NZ165 from Auckland said he thought he was travelling to Western Australia.

"I got confused, I saw Western Sydney," he said.

"I thought it was Western Australia, and I'm meant to be in Perth, but look, it's still pretty fun, so we'll make the best of it.

"I realised by the time I got on the flight that that's not where it was going, but we'll figure it out.

"I'm on holiday, so it's not the worst thing."

Weighing up if a trip from Sydney's new airport is for you The doors to Western Sydney International Airport are set to soon welcome commercial passengers.

Some of the first passengers to travel through WSI have praised the new $5.6 billion airport terminal's layout and operation.

Three domestic Jetstar flights are scheduled for today, with Air New Zealand flights this morning marking the first international departure and arrivals.

Seven carriers have signed up to operate out of WSI.

Flights to Singapore are scheduled to start soon, with other destinations including Nadi in Fiji, Ho Chi Minh City and Doha to follow.

title: Youth boxing program fights off negativity, provides positive role models
text:
Encouraging young boys to put on gloves and fight each other inside a boxing ring may not seem like the most obvious way to keep them out of trouble at first glance.

But those behind this weekend's amateur Gloves of Hope challenge in Darwin would argue the sport is helping do just that, and much more, for young people in the Northern Territory.

The event is an initiative of local grassroots organisation Hoops 4 Health — an Aboriginal-led service behind several sport programs designed to support struggling youth, including some inside NT detention centres.

The sold-out event saw boxers from across the region compete at Marrara Stadium. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

The free Gloves of Hope program aims to give young men and women a chance to learn boxing skills from professional coaches while building resilience, discipline and a support network in their community.

"We try to improve their mental health, but also guide them with integrity about how they live their lives," social impact director Matthew Bonson said.

Mr Bonson said the program was based on evidence-backed models of therapy which use patterned, rhythmic exercise to help trauma-affected youth regulate their emotions.

Matthew Bonson says the patterned, rhythmic exercise has been shown to help with emotional regulation. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

"Through sport and the structures around good coaches, you can help these young men stay cool longer and also help young women get more confidence about who they are," he said.

As the NT grapples with some of the highest youth incarceration rates in the country, particularly among First Nations boys aged 10 to 14, Mr Bonson said providing young people with positive role models was a key part of the program's success.

While the program is "not a magic-wand solution", Mr Bonson says it exposes the young boxers to positive role models. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

"Particularly with young men, if you put the right older men in front of them — who they know are trying to help them — they do want to listen," Mr Bonson said.

" It's not a magic-wand solution, but we're trying our best to give [young people] positive examples. "

Territory boxing talent on show

On Saturday, Gloves of Hope teamed up with Boxing NT to host one of Darwin's biggest amateur boxing events of the last decade.

The sold-out event at Marrara Stadium brought together boxing clubs from across Darwin and Alice Springs, with one team even travelling from Kununurra in Western Australia.

Declan Unwin-Walker was one of the fighters competing for the title belt on Saturday and said he was "keen, excited, nervous — but ready to go".

Declan Unwin-Walker says Gloves of Hope is all about supporting each other and encouraging fellow boxers to continue showing up. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

Mr Unwin-Walker trained with Gloves of Hope for more than a year in the lead-up to the event and said the sport had been rewarding, physically and mentally.

"We all push each other and show up every day and its definitely about pushing each other and just yeah — keep showing up," he said.

Jerrel O'Riley from the Kununurra Warriors Boxing Club said it was exciting to compete on a big stage.

Jerrel O'Riley and his team were visiting from Kununurra in Western Australia, with plenty of representation from rural Darwin clubs in attendance too. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

"I was pretty surprised to hear there was 1,000 people coming," he told the ABC ahead of the sold-out event.

" That's the main thing I'm worried about, getting knocked out in front of 1,000 people. "

Richard Garling, who has coached the sport for more than four decades, was there on behalf of the Humpty Doo Boxing Club.

Mr Garling said pathways into boxing that helped kids from rural areas compete were essential to fostering NT talent.

Mr Garling hopes events like this will encourage young boxers to continue on their journey, going on to compete in even bigger competitions over time. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

"There's a lot of potential in the Territory," he said.

" Hopefully all these kids tonight can continue their journey somewhere higher — state titles, national titles or Golden Gloves. "

The event also featured a half-time performance by NT music star Yung Milla, fresh from his triumph on reality music competition show The Voice Australia.

The funds raised from ticket sales were donated to help the Gloves of Hope initiative, with organisers hopeful the event will return next year.

title: Fowler's City draw to end winning start
text:
Manchester United striker Elisabeth Terland scored a late equaliser to knock visitors Manchester City off top spot in the Women's Super League table on Sunday evening as a hotly contested derby finished 1-1 at the Leigh Sports Ground.

Matildas star Mary Fowler slid the ball to Bunny Shaw to open the scoring for the champions in the 66th minute.

Making her 100th WSL appearance, Shaw brushed off the challenge of Dominique Janssen and powered a shot into the far corner to break the deadlock and silence the home fans, who booed and heckled her throughout.

However, Norway international Terland was on hand to blast the ball into the net to grab a point for her side in the 89th minute of the game.

It was the first time that City has dropped points this season, allowing Ellie Carpenter's Chelsea to go top on goal difference after it came back from a goal down to beat Crystal Palace 3-1 earlier in the day.

Ellie Carpenter had to battle hard for Chelsea. (Getty Images: WSL/Tom Dulat)

Chelsea and City both have 19 points, with London City Lionesses third on 16 and Manchester United fourth on 11.

On Merseyside, Liverpool's Jana Fernandez Velasco struck deep into stoppage time to snatch a 2-2 draw at home to London City.

Aston Villa raced out to a 3-0 lead over Everton by the 50th minute with Amalie Vangsgaard scoring twice, but the home side scored twice late on to ensure a nervous finish as Villa held on for a 3-2 win.

Charlton Athletic's miserable run continued as it slumped to its seventh straight defeat.

Substitute Wilma Leidhammar scored the only goal of the game for Birmingham City in the 68th minute to leave Charlton, who counts Matildas veteran Emily van Egmond among its ranks, still firmly rooted to the bottom of the table and searching for its first point of the season.

title: Labor promises $6.8b South Coast rail fix days after timetable backflip
text:
The New South Wales government has promised to deliver a $6.8 billion upgrade to the South Coast rail line if re-elected next year, days after scrapping a controversial new timetable that would have added more trains for Illawarra commuters.

The plan includes a commitment to deliver on a promise made by Labor at the 2005 NSW election to electrify the line between Kiama and Bomaderry.

That would allow passengers to travel from Sydney to Nowra without changing to the diesel train currently completing the journey.

The South Coast Rail Plan also includes extra tracks and passing loops between Wollongong and Kiama, and a doubling of the tracks between Hurstville and Sutherland to separate passenger and freight trains.

Transport Minister John Graham said splitting the services would make an enormous difference.

"That will be a big boost then to what's possible," he said.

"At the moment that's a real constraint on the network that will allow a service uplift for this whole line."

Planning is expected to start in 2027, with construction to be completed by the mid to late 2030s.

The announcement was made days after a planned timetable overhaul on the line was scrapped. (ABC News)

Minister for the Illawarra Ryan Park described the upgrade as a "must-have" on a line that was expected to see passenger demand grow by almost 30 per cent by 2041.

The announcement came just two days after the NSW government scrapped its November timetable overhaul following backlash from commuters who faced longer travel times and the loss of an airport connection at Wolli Creek, in exchange for more frequent T4 and South Coast services.

Mr Park said no alternative changes to improve the line were being considered in the short term, and the upgrade was the priority.

The government has described the project as the largest heavy rail infrastructure commitment in generations for the Illawarra and South Coast, and one that has been long-awaited.

Chris Minns announced the upgrade commitment in Bomaderry this morning. (ABC Illawarra: Charles Rushforth)

Long time coming

Premier Chris Minns noted there might be cynicism from the public following decades of promised upgrades that had not been delivered.

"There's some people who will never believe it until they jump on an electrified train from Bomaderry," he said.

As well as the 2005 commitment, a version of the upgrade was proposed ahead of the 2019 election by then-Liberal incumbent Gareth Ward.

That plan was scrapped in 2023 by the new Labor government and the opposition.

"I'm hoping we can draw on some of the goodwill associated with previous projects that we said we'd deliver and we have, to bring some confidence," the Premier said.

South Coast Labor MP Liza Butler said the announcement marked a game-changing investment in regional transport.

"We have seen money tunnelled into Sydney Metro while we have been left behind. Well, no more," she said.

The project also includes $621 million in early infrastructure upgrades to the line.

Some of those upgrades have already begun, with funding allocated in the most recent state budget as part of the Illawarra Rail Resilience Plan.

Rod Watson says the upgrade will be excellent for the line. (ABC Illawarra: Charles Rushforth)

Rod Watson uses the south coast line frequently to visit family in North Nowra.

"I think it would be excellent. This is a very, very busy line when I travel on it," he said.

At Bomaderry Station this morning, passenger Denis said the upgrade "seemed like a sensible thing to do".

"It seems like it probably should have been done quite a while ago," he said.

Fran and Denis were two passengers at Bomaderry station who welcomed the election pledge. (ABC Illawarra: Charles Rushforth)

Fellow passenger Fran said the upgrade would improve her trip from the airport to visit grandchildren on the South Coast, which currently takes three and a half hours and involves three changes.

Unions anticipate job boost

Rail Tram and Bus Union president Craig Turner said the project would create hundreds of jobs during and after construction.

"They will have to have more train crews because there will be more trains, which is great," he said.

Mr Turner said the unions had been advocating for the upgrade for decades.

title: England 'gutted' after second extraordinary ODI defeat in as many games
text:
Shadab Khan hit an epic ODI century, and England suffered a second extraordinary defeat in as many games as Pakistan snatched a one-wicket victory on Sunday to secure its place in the cricket tri-series final.

Pakistan's chase looked doomed at 9-154 before a defiant 89-run, last-wicket stand between Shadab and number 11 Haris Rauf secured Pakistan a dazzling win. Shadab smashed his first one-day ton to take Pakistan to 9-243 in 47.1 overs.

Even within that 10th-wicket stand, Pakistan seemed to have been beaten when Gus Atkinson won an LBW decision against Shadab with 21 runs still required.

Shadab threw his bat down and started congratulating England's players before asking for a speculative review, which showed the faintest inside edge, leaving Shadab screaming with joy at the reprieve.

"The boys are absolutely gutted," England coach Brendon McCullum told the BBC.

"Today they fought incredibly hard … we were in a pretty good position, well, a very good position and then obviously we weren't able to get across the line.

"The last game was, the boys were gutted after that, and you look in the dressing room now, they're also extremely gutted now."

England, which scored 429 and still lost in its last game against Sri Lanka, was earlier all out for 241 in 46.4 overs.

Playing his first game in the tournament, Shadab scored 113 not out off 96 balls and farmed most of the strike. Rauf (7 not out in 19 balls) hit the winning boundary as Pakistan enjoyed its third successive win.

It was the biggest last-wicket partnership in a successful chase in ODIs.

The 10th-wicket partnership was the largest ever to win a game in ODI cricket. (Getty Images: Sameer Ali)

Left-handed opener Ben Duckett scored 105 for England — his fifth ODI century and first against Pakistan — after Shaheen Shah Afridi won his first toss in the tournament and elected to field after successfully defending 300-plus scores in the first two games.

It was England's third successive defeat in the tournament after losing to Pakistan by 87 runs and seeing Sri Lanka pull off the second-highest successful run chase in ODI history despite captain Harry Brook scoring a blistering 114-ball double century.

Pakistan will take on Sri Lanka in their last league game on Tuesday after beating the Sri Lankans by 37 runs in the opening game.

Rauf joined Shadab at 9-154 in the 34th over and launched a partnership neither side will quickly forget. While Shadab outsmarted England pace with his brilliant batting, Rauf gave him ample support by sensibly not going for expansive shots.

Shadab protected Rauf well by keeping the strike to himself and counterpunching the bowlers by hitting boundaries early in the over, completing his century by playing a late cut off Atkinson for his 12th boundary before hitting the fast bowler over long off for a six to reduce the target to three runs off the final three overs.

Rauf drilled debutant fast bowler Henry Crocombe for a straight boundary to cap a remarkable recovery for Pakistan.

Earlier, Jamie Overton (3-43) took two smart slip catches to remove both struggling opening batters Fakhar Zaman (10) and Saim Ayub (6) and Babar Azam will continue his search for a big innings after Atkinson pegged back his off stump as Pakistan slumped to 3-31 inside the first seven overs.

Brook then turned to Overton soon after the batting power play, and the fast bowler responded immediately in his first over when 19-year-old Saad Baig (32) cut straight to Will Jacks at point.

Left-arm spinner Liam Dawson (2-30) and Jacks (1-18) then bowled tidily and raised England's hopes of their first win.

Duckett revived England from a precarious 4-52 with a 93-run stand with Sam Curran, who made 42 off 52 balls.

Afridi picked up 4-46 and England lost four of the five top batters for single digits. That included the run-out of Brook, who went for a second run but fell short of his crease to an electrifying throw from debutant Razaullah.

England lost quick wickets and slipped to 9-201 after Afridi removed Curran in his return spell when he holed out to fine leg off a mistimed pull. Razaullah took 2-38, grabbing the wickets of Jacks and Dawson.

Duckett, who hit 10 fours and two sixes in his 111-ball knock, fell in the 37th over when he top-edged a sweep to fine leg against left-arm spinner Arafat Minhas before Atkinson (36 not out) shared a 40-run last-wicket stand with Crocombe.

AP/ABC

Key points DANCE: The Australian Ballet returns to the State Theatre with The Nutcracker

JAZZ: Melbourne International Jazz festival wraps up for another year

MUSIC: Melbourne Chamber Orchestra performs Twilight Dialogues

MUSIC: Louis Tomlinson puts on a big show at John Cain Arena

DANCE

The Nutcracker ★★★★

The Australian Ballet, Ian Potter State Theatre, Arts Centre Melbourne, until October 31 The State Theatre has reopened after 2½ years of renovations, and Arts Centre Melbourne is keen to reassure audiences that its familiar character survives. The Australian Ballet has taken the hint, returning home with Peter Wright’s The Nutcracker, created for Birmingham Royal Ballet in 1990: an old favourite offering reassurance on a suitably extravagant scale. Yuumi Yamada as Clara in The Nutcracker. Kate Longley John F. Macfarlane’s gigantic, dreamy designs seem almost to have grown out of the theatre. The Stahlbaums’ drawing room, swathed in dark red curtains, extends the auditorium’s crimson plush into the family Christmas party. With festive decorations glistering like seams of emerald in the shadows, the whole experience feels deliciously subterranean: a theatre and a household tucked into the same deep burrow. We’re all here underground together. Yuumi Yamada supplies the youthful enthusiasm this cosy fantasy needs. Her Clara, a ballet student dreaming herself into a ballerina, is eager, unguarded and winsomely adolescent, and her delight in everything has an attractive freedom. Jarryd Madden’s fatherly Drosselmeyer offers a steadying presence.

Advertisement

The finest enchantment in this version remains Wright’s reimagined version of the Dance of the Snowflakes at the end of the first act, led here by Isobelle Dashwood’s graceful Snow Fairy. On Saturday night, the second act sometimes felt rushed. The national dances were briskly dispatched, and the Waltz of the Flowers grew a little unruly, the ensemble’s lines scattering beneath Macfarlane’s overhead tangle of streamers. Intentional or otherwise, the visual rhyme was actually quite enjoyable: the flowers and their consorts seemed to have caught the delirium of the decoration. But the entrance of Sharni Spencer’s queenly Sugar Plum Fairy soon restored order. The battle beneath the Christmas tree impresses. Kate Longley The theatre itself still smells new. The seats are a considerable improvement, although the space between rows feels even more miserly than before. The additional aisles do, however, offer more accessibility. The gridlock in the stalls after the curtain comes down is now, I hope, a thing of the past. The acoustics require a more cautious verdict after one visit, but, still, Orchestra Victoria – led by Jonathan Lo – sounded very good to me, with a notably crisp brass section. Familiarity has its attractions and there is still plenty in this production – such as the battle beneath the Christmas tree – that impresses. On the other hand, after nearly two decades and five seasons in The Australian Ballet’s repertoire, this Nutcracker is starting to feel a little old-fashioned. The building has had its renovation – now for the ballet?

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann

Advertisement

JAZZ

Melbourne International Jazz Festival

Closing weekend, October 23–25 When Tigran Hamasyan was a child, he dreamed of playing guitar in a heavy-metal band. On stage last Friday, he was playing piano in a recital hall rather than shredding on electric guitar for a moshpit full of metalheads, but his incendiary concert left us in no doubt that his childhood ambition was still lodged firmly in his heart and hands. Tigran Hamasyan performs at MIJF Will Hamilton Coates Volume, velocity and virtuosity were the hallmarks of his quartet’s performance on the closing weekend of this year’s Melbourne International Jazz Festival. The delicacy and ethereal beauty that defined Hamasyan’s solo show at the festival in 2017 surfaced occasionally, via hushed melodies and haunting echoes of Armenian folk music. But for every glimpse of light and nuance, there were a hundred frantic runs and pummelling chords, with thundering drums and a bass sound so penetrating that its vibrations were felt more than heard. This was music as extreme sport, the players executing mind-bending rhythmic puzzles and building elaborate, interlocking motifs with astonishing synchronicity as they expanded on the bold vision of Hamasyan’s album Manifeste. Often using his piano as a percussion instrument, Hamasyan pounded the keys with visceral intensity as he sparred with Yessaï Karapetian’s churning keyboards or locked in tight with the jagged momentum of Marc Karapetian’s bass and Arman Mnatsakanyan’s drums.

Advertisement

Witnessing the band at full force felt like riding bareback on a runaway stallion while clinging on for dear life, or being tossed about in a dark, roiling ocean filled with unpredictable currents. It was gripping and immersive, exhilarating and exhausting – a fascinating window into the ever-mutating world of this unique artist. One of the festival’s biggest names, Dee Dee Bridgewater, was scheduled to perform on Saturday, but the US singer withdrew from the festival just days before her concert due to ill health. Losing an international headliner will undoubtedly have left a sizeable dent in the festival’s coffers, but there was still plenty of exceptional music on offer that day. The 10th anniversary of the album Aziza was celebrated as part of this year’s festival. Duncographic The morning drizzle cleared and the clouds parted just in time for Mandisi Dyantyis’ outdoor show in Prahran Square. The South African trumpeter and singer fronted a superb nine-piece local band – Afrospace Interchange – that helped bring Dyantyis’ vibrant music to life. Warm and impassioned, Dyantyis roamed the stage or used gestures to communicate the story of each song, buoyed by the band’s exuberant rhythms, majestic horns and uplifting vocal harmonies. Later that night, American cellist-composer Tomeka Reid and her quartet gave a riveting performance in the newly opened second room at JazzLab – a seriously impressive venue that’s twice the size of the original room while still retaining an air of intimacy.

Advertisement

Drawing on their latest album, dance! skip! hop!, Reid and her remarkable colleagues (guitarist Mary Halvorson, bassist Jason Roebke and drummer Tomas Fujiwara) navigated the leader’s intricate compositions with supreme precision, though the arrangements still left room for spontaneous interplay. This was a highly collaborative affair, with all four instruments given equal prominence. Roles were fluid, too: Reid’s cello could mimic sonorous basslines, pluck deft harmonies or maintain an earthy pulse as her colleagues darted nimbly around her. Her interactions with Halvorson were especially vivid, the pair moving in deft unison or harmony, or conversing in improvised spurts as Halvorson added pitch-bending slides and expressive smears. On Sunday night, bassist and composer Dave Holland – a seminal figure in jazz for more than half a century – took to the stage with three contemporary masters of the genre: saxophonist Chris Potter, guitarist Lionel Loueke and drummer Eric Harland. Reuniting to celebrate the 10th anniversary of their album Aziza, the quartet revisited the repertoire from that album with thrilling vitality. Holland’s agile basslines anchored each piece with effortless authority, underlining the funky swagger of Aziza Dance, the airy calypso shuffle of Summer 15 and the complex metric variations of Blue Sufi. The final number was infused with an upbeat Afro-Latin feel, Loueke trading animated phrases with Potter’s muscular tenor over the rhythm section’s bustling propulsion. The tune? Sleepless Nights – an apt title for patrons who’ve filled their past ten days and nights with memorable music, and a fitting way to farewell this year’s festival.

Reviewed by Jessica Nicholas

MUSIC

Twilight Dialogues ★★★★

Melbourne Chamber Orchestra, 75 Reid St, October 25 Frequent reminders we live in the country with the oldest continuous music practice in the world have hopefully set stale notions about “old world” and “new world” art on their head. The Melbourne Chamber Orchestra performs Twilight Dialogues. Albert Comper This polished and engaging program of clarinet quintets in which Brahms’ beloved work in the genre was preceded by Songs from the Bush written by Melbourne-born pianist and composer Ian Munro, explored subtle connections between European and Australian art music. Dating from 2009, Munro’s three-movement score reveals a masterly grasp of classic chamber music writing, offering intriguing changes of mood and texture. Incorporating folk tunes collected mid last century and an adapted Walmajarri children’s song, he creates a uniquely Australian soundscape.

Advertisement

Country Dance incorporates an unnamed Irish jig while Campfire and Night Sky reimagines classic night music with a freewheeling clarinet over gentle pulsing, muted strings. A Drover’s Lament summons up the pathos of the lonely immigrant before final percussive string effects suggest a ticking clock and the reminiscence of celebrations long ago, whether Indigenous or colonial. David Griffiths’ mellifluous and multi-hued clarinet eloquently voiced the music’s emotional flow, enjoying a fine rapport with the string quartet formed of principals from the Melbourne Chamber Orchestra, especially first violin Sophie Rowell. Together with the other members of the ensemble (violinist Kathryn Taylor, violist Merewyn Bramble and cellist Blair Harris), the Brahms was given a vivid, nuanced performance. The opening tension between restive drama and questing lyricism was well established, while Griffiths excelled in releasing the passionate heartache of the Adagio, muted strings recalling Munro’s use of the same effect. Highly characterised, the sunnier Andantino and the finale’s set of variations demonstrated the players’ tightly knit synergy. Part of the dynamic artistic leadership Rowell brings to the entire MCO enterprise, thought-provoking chamber music concerts such as this are a welcome bonus.

Reviewed by Tony Way

Advertisement

MUSIC

Louis Tomlinson ★★★★

John Cain Arena, October 20 The screams that greet Louis Tomlinson give me a contact high. Die-hard fans have legged it to the barrier and thrust stage. The word “Lemonade” flashes on-screen, towering over Tomlinson and his five-piece band. He cuts an amiable, Gallagher-type figure in a puffy red jacket and jeans. Until he’s briefly engulfed in a confetti explosion. Louis Tomlinson performing at John Cain Arena on October 20. Richard Clifford Music videos are composed live, faces projected dystopia-large with film effects, high-contrast overlays or psychedelic sunflowers, with colour-saturated stage lights and even a synth-laser show for Broken Bones. It’s a leap from the opening act, Rum Jungle, the kind of Aussie indie group you play driving to the beach on P-plates with your mates.

Advertisement

Tomlinson gets somewhat swallowed in the production. The mixing does no favours, his piping, Arctic Monkeys-style vocals no match for thundering drums in songs like The Spark. He’s often lost in backing harmonies and the word-faithful crowd, unless it’s the pared-back cover of the Foo Fighters’ My Hero. But Tomlinson’s impeccable band shines. Oozing rock, they unify eclectic leaps from funk pop and acoustic ballads to nostalgic indie/Britpop like the Oasis-esque Saturdays and Franz Ferdinand-style dance riffs in Out of my System. Keyboard skips between plinking piano and glimmering synth as the guitarists and bassist pace like tigers to tumbling, chest-shaking beats and rip blistering solos. The word “Lemonade” flashes on-screen over Tomlinson and his five-piece band. Richard Clifford Tomlinson performs a pop persona perfectly. Gracious and grateful. Hand on heart, pointing to swooning fans. His grinning, Yorkshire-accented commentary is lightly peppered with profanities: “Loud as you fooken’ can!” In return, the One Direction star is utterly adored. For One Direction’s Night Changes, a sea of phones rise, recording intently. Tomlinson’s grim-faced guards have to pull him back from the barrier when ladies get grabby in the encore. I only wonder if he regretted the jacket in the fervent, feminine body heat filling John Cain Arena.

Red Metal Limited has put another piece of a key metallurgical puzzle in place at its massive Sybella rare earths project near Mount Isa in Queensland, with impressive column leach test results from the Kary Zone’s deeper, more dominant fresh granite ore. The company says two-metre column leach tests on the granite, crushed to 10 millimetres, achieved solid neodymium and praseodymium recoveries of 65 per cent and 68 per cent, respectively. Notably, the result was achieved with a total acid consumption of just 19 kilograms per tonne of sulphuric acid at ambient temperature, which is materially lower than the 23–27kg used in tests for the two other weathered ore types that sit above it. Surface granite (pictured) at Red Metal Limited’s Sybella project sitting just 20km from the major mining hub of Mount Isa in Queensland. Neodymium and praseodymium are particularly valuable because they are used to manufacture powerful permanent magnets for electric vehicles, wind turbines and industrial equipment. In heap leaching, a chemical solution is trickled through the crushed ore to dissolve the valuable metals, which are then collected from the liquid and recovered. Low acid consumption is important because acid can be one of the biggest costs in heap leaching.

Advertisement

‘The new data will feed into our current Sybella PFS to assess the potential economics of this very large rare earth project.’ Red Metal Limited managing director Rob Rutherford The fresh granite accounts for the lion’s share of the Kary Zone’s monster 936-million-tonne (Mt) inferred mineral resource, weighing in at 598Mt, while the overlying saprock and transitional ores contribute 182Mt and 157Mt respectively. With all three ore types now successfully tested, the company appears to have cleared a major hurdle on its path to a prefeasibility study (PFS). The Kary Zone resource currently grades 334 parts per million (ppm) neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) and 31.7ppm dysprosium-terbium (DyTb) at a 300ppm NdPr cut-off. Intriguingly, the mineralisation remains open at depth, with drilling encountering rare earths down to 240 metres, suggesting the deposit could potentially become bigger with further drilling. Meanwhile, the company is running a separate test using 20mm crushed ore packed into 150mm-diameter columns standing six metres tall to closely replicate the conditions of a commercial heap leach pad. The final results are expected to build on Red Metal’s previously successful two-metre column program, which delivered impressive neodymium recoveries of 76 per cent from transitional ore and 71 per cent from saprock. Praseodymium recoveries were equally encouraging, reaching 78 per cent and 72 per cent from the respective ore types. Red Metal Limited managing director Rob Rutherford said: “The positive column leach test on the fresh granite mineralisation from the Kary Zone has demonstrated the heap leach potential of the very large fresh granite resource located immediately below the near-surface, saprock and transitional ores which remains open at depth.”

Advertisement

In parallel with its metallurgical work, the company has drill rods already turning on a 5000-metre campaign aiming to both upgrade and extend the Kary Zone deposit. Infill drilling is targeting near-surface, rich zones, while extensional drilling is testing the interpreted southeast extension where previous work hinted at higher-grade potential. Management describes the Sybella deposit as geologically unique, with abundant granite-hosted soft ore, giving the project a compelling edge and offering simple crushing and processing options. Sybella lies in a 12km long by 3km wide granite-pervasive corridor and holds an enormous global resource of 4.795 billion tonnes grading 302ppm NdPr. These metals sit alongside the more valuable heavy rare earths dysprosium and terbium at a combined 28ppm, with yttrium adding a further 136ppm. The results have landed at an opportune time, as Australia and its allies ramp up efforts to loosen China’s grip on global rare earths supply chains, with government-backed financing and strategic-reserve measures increasingly focused on the critical minerals sector. Against that backdrop, a large, shallow, granite-hosted resource that has demonstrated ambient-temperature heap-leach potential - and includes both light and heavy magnet rare earths - is likely to attract attention. While Sybella is the clear flagship, Red Metal is also pursuing a “Big Copper” strategy in the famed Mt Isa province, hunting for giant iron-oxide-copper-gold discoveries similar to the nearby Ernest Henry and Osborne deposits. The company recently expanded its footprint in the region, lodging 17 new tenement applications near its Gulf and Three Ways projects to bring its total landholding to a vast 5800 square kilometres.

Advertisement

The company is also running a high-resolution airborne gravity survey at Mt Isa, piggybacking on concurrent regional airborne gravity surveys conducted by the Geological Survey of Queensland and Geoscience Australia. With metallurgical work de-risking its processing pathway, drills turning to expand its already giant resource and a separate hunt for monster copper deposits underway, Red Metal looks to be firing on all cylinders. The completion of the Sybella PFS, slated for the first quarter of 2027 and results from the six-metre column test will likely be the next key catalysts as the company sketches out the economics of its potentially world-class asset. Gawn is off contract in 2027, but at 33 is still playing some of the best football of his career, which he attributes, in part, to his punishing off-season cycling regime. Melbourne captain Max Gawn cycles alongside Tour de France champion Cadel Evans ahead of the Great Ocean Road race. There are two other games scheduled at the Adelaide Oval across the weekend – Sydney v Collingwood on the Friday night and an early Saturday game between Carlton and Melbourne, who met in a wildcard final in 2026. Gold Coast, GWS, Geelong and St Kilda are the four teams heading to the Barossa for their Gather Round games, while Richmond, West Coast, Essendon and North Melbourne are bound for Norwood Oval. Look away, Port fans: Zak Butters in Western Bulldogs colours. Getty Images South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas – an avid Power fan – was quick to spruik the Gather Round program, which coincides with the Easter school holidays, and the inclusion of a players’ parade on the Friday. “The blockbuster weekend of footy will be boosted with the inaugural Players Parade on Friday, allowing fans to see their heroes from all 18 clubs in one spot,” he said. “Personally, I’m looking forward to being at a packed Adelaide Oval to see Zak Butters take on his former teammates.”

Dean Solomon as coach of Essendon. Getty Images Solomon, now 46, was on the coaching staff at the Suns from the club’s inception in the AFL in 2011 to 2020, even serving three games as interim coach following the departure of Rodney Eade in 2017. Solomon later joined the board at Essendon – the club where he made his name as a player and was part of the 2000 premiership team – but relinquished that position a year ago to return to a hands-on coaching role.

He started the 2026 season as an assistant to Brad Scott, and became the club’s stop-gap coach when Scott was sacked mid-season. title: James Packer pays $1.8m to law firm also defending Netanyahu’s corruption charges
