Billionaire James Packer has paid at least $US1.25 million ($1.78 million) to the Tel Aviv law firm also defending Benjamin Netanyahu against allegations the Israeli prime minister corruptly received benefits from the Australian businessman and other wealthy supporters a decade ago. An investigation by this masthead on the eve of seismic Israeli elections has uncovered a money trail involving monthly $US50,000 wire transfers over the past two years from a bank account controlled by Packer’s company to the account of Netanyahu’s legal defence firm. Australian businessman James Packer (left) and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Aresna Villanueva The first monthly “retainer” payment from the Citibank account of Packer’s firm Consolidated Press International was made on September 23, 2024 to the account of law firm Hadad Roth Shenhar at Israel’s Mizrahi Tefahot bank. The monthly payments, which Packer has not denied, have continued for two years. A source aware of the payments, but not authorised to speak publicly, said they should be urgently investigated to determine if Netanyahu was receiving an undisclosed benefit from Packer as the law firm defends the Israeli prime minister over allegations he unlawfully accepted expensive gifts from Packer between 2014 and 2016.

Advertisement

Israeli authorities have repeatedly blocked Netanyahu from receiving funds from wealthy backers to pay for his defence in his long-running corruption case. This masthead has not confirmed that Netanyahu benefited from the payments. Editor's pick Courts Star chefs, cigars and pink champagne: How James Packer made a mark in Israel If it was found Packer’s payments to the law firm directly or indirectly benefited Netanyahu, the source alleged the payments could involve fresh breaches of Israeli laws governing how politicians can accept support, and might also fall under US laws that govern financial transactions or possible benefits foreign politicians receive from businesses. Asked about the allegations on Monday morning, a spokesperson for Netanyahu said: “I couldn’t give a monkey’s about your questions. “We are very busy. We have an election on right now.”

Advertisement

When contacted by this masthead on Friday night, Packer did not deny the rolling $US50,000 payments but declined to comment. A source familiar with the 59-year-old former media mogul’s financial dealings later insisted the wire transfers to Netanyahu’s lawyers were for work done for Packer – including “deal finding” in Israel where Packer has business interests – and unrelated to the prime minister’s court case. Netanyahu (left) and Packer (right) at the United Nations in 2016. Ten News This masthead subsequently requested evidence of any deals in Israel or work undertaken by the law firm, but neither Packer nor his company have yet responded. In addition to running Netanyahu’s defence against claims the Israeli leader broke his country’s law by accepting luxury goods from Packer and wealthy film producer Arnon Milchan, law firm Hadad Roth Shenhar is helping Netanyahu contest allegations that he improperly traded favours with an Israeli newspaper publisher and telecommunications company.

Advertisement

Netanyahu’s primary defence attorney is Hadad Roth Shenhar’s most senior lawyer, Amit Hadad. Hadad has gained prominence by appearing for several Israeli government ministers and business identities, but Netanyahu is his most notable client. Netanyahu in 2024 with lawyer Amit Hadad (right). AP Hadad did not respond to questions from this masthead. In addition to the ongoing corruption trial, Netanyahu has controversially, and unsuccessfully, sought legal permission allowing his wealthy overseas friends to fund the law firm Hadad Roth Shenhar. Israeli authorities have ruled Netanyahu cannot rely on the rich backers because this would amount to a breach of trust and conflict of interest.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Updated

Courts Netanyahu assails media as he testifies for first time in his corruption trial Transparency International said Packer’s decision to pay $US1.25 million to the law firm defending Netanyahu demanded urgent and independent scrutiny. “As there are already significant corruption charges against Mr Netanyahu relating to past gifts from Mr Packer, and other business associates, these new allegations must be thoroughly investigated by authorities,” said Transparency International’s Australian director, Clancy Moore. Moore also cautioned that evidence might yet show the payments were unrelated to Netanyahu. Moore stressed scrutiny was also required in light of the previous concerns about who could pay for Netanyahu’s legal fees. “Significantly, Israeli authorities have repeatedly ruled that Mr Netanyahu can’t use funds from foreign benefactors to fund his legal defence against corruption charges due to conflict of interests and his failure to disclose his wealth,” Moore said.

Advertisement

Packer found himself entangled in Netanyahu’s corruption case after gifting the prime minister champagne and cigars more than a decade ago, but has not been accused of any wrongdoing and has not been called as a witness to the prime minister’s corruption trial. An aerial view of the beachside villas Benjamin Netanyahu (left in circle) and James Packer owned in the gated community on Hadar Street, in Caesarea, about 45 minutes north of Tel Aviv, Israel. Google Maps Packer and Netanyahu at the time lived in neighbouring villas in the exclusive township of Caesarea and were regular guests at each other’s homes. Netanyahu even had a key to Packer’s luxury property. Packer once called the Israeli prime minister “probably the most impressive man I’ve ever met”. Australian Federal Police officers interviewed Packer on behalf of their Israeli counterparts in late 2017 but stressed he was a witness in the case – not a suspect – and that he co-operated fully.

Advertisement

Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict October 7 changed their lives. Now they are running for office This masthead submitted detailed questions to Packer’s privately owned Consolidated Press Holdings (CPH). The company did not reply. The questions included whether it was appropriate for Packer to make payments to Netanyahu’s law firm given it was defending him in a case which involved the Australian businessman, and why Hadad Roth Shenhar was selected for investment advice. Consolidated Press International (CPI) is one of several private investment arms operated by Packer. At the time that payments to Netanyahu’s law firm began, CPI had more than $600 million in investments in technology companies including Taiwan semiconductor Nvidia and Facebook owner Meta. Packer later pivoted to gambling stocks through large stakes in Las Vegas-based poker machine manufacturer Light and Wonder, and Sportsbet’s parent company Flutter. He has also invested heavily in AI.

Advertisement

Tuesday’s election in Israel represents a crucial juncture for the Middle East, with Netanyahu’s right-wing government facing potential defeat. His removal from office would trigger a reset of the conflicts in Iran and Gaza and redraw the relationship between Jerusalem and US President Donald Trump. Packer and film producer Arnon Milchan (centre) listen to Netanyahu speak at a joint meeting of the US Congress in 2015. Getty Netanyahu – Israel’s longest serving prime minister and the country’s first sitting leader to be charged with a crime – has repeatedly invoked the security situation in the Middle East to argue for delays in giving evidence at his corruption trial. Known as Case 1000, Netanyahu was in 2019 indicted on fraud and breach of trust charges for accepting luxury gifts from Packer and film producer Arnon Milchan worth about $295,000. Netanyahu is also accused of intervening on behalf of Milchan for various business matters, including a US visa renewal. The first international commercial flight has flown from Western Sydney International to Auckland, New Zealand. WSI’s first domestic flight – a Jetstar flight to the Gold Coast – took place yesterday. The plane had touched down earlier on Monday at Western Sydney International (WSI), arriving from Auckland at 7.27am. The trans-Tasman flight marks the start of the airline’s travel to WSI, where it will fly three times weekly from Auckland. Matt and Serena Ross are among the passengers on the flight to Auckland. In keeping with the Air New Zealand brand, the flight featured headrest coverings emblazoned with the words “First Flight Feels”.

title: Venezuela's most prominent opposition leader returns home from exile
text:
In brief Venezuela's opposition leader has made a dramatic return from exile.

Her homecoming could reshape the country's political future.

María Corina Machado, Venezuela's primary opposition leader and a Nobel Peace Prize winner, made a surprise return home on Monday after nearly a year in exile, drawing jubilant crowds in a direct challenge to the United States-backed interim government.

Thousands of people lined highways, toll plazas and city streets waving Venezuelan flags and chanting "Liberty!" as Machado travelled toward Caracas in a convoy of cars and motorbikes.

In Guacara, the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency witnessed Machado singing the national anthem as supporters packed out a plaza, waving flags and cheering her return.

Wearing her trademark white T-shirt and blue jeans, she leaned through the sunroof of a vehicle to wave to the crowds.

A woman shouted, "Maria, if you come back, my daughter has to come back!" referring to one of the millions of Venezuelans who have fled repression and a moribund economy.

Her return puts Venezuela's most influential opposition figure back at the centre of the country's tumultuous politics.

Machado slipped out of the country last December to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, after spending nearly a year in hiding.

Since then, the 59-year-old has made at least seven unsuccessful attempts to return to Venezuela, according to sources in her party.

She finally reappeared on Monday at the Santa Rosa church in the western city of Barquisimeto, where supporters greeted her with chants of "Viva Maria Corina!"

Return from exile

Two Venezuelan exiles told AFP she had entered the country from neighbouring Colombia, although Colombian authorities did not immediately confirm that account.

She returns to a country much changed — nine months ago her nemesis president Nicolás Maduro was captured in a US military operation and jailed in the US.

But to the democratic opposition's dismay, his deputy Delcy Rodríguez took over as interim president, with the US' blessing.

Since then, the Nobel laureate has been forced to watch from exile in Panama as US-backed talks on a political transition took place without her.

The interim government has promised elections but has not yet set a date.

Machado has repeatedly praised US President Donald Trump for launching the risky operation, and even gifted him the Nobel medal she received.

Trump has repeatedly expressed satisfaction with Rodriguez as she fulfils key US demands, particularly on granting access to Venezuelan oil.

Trump said Sunday he was not aware of Machado's return, adding: "But I think she's a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel prize, so how can I say anything else?"

"We're doing very well in Venezuela," he said.

US secretary of state Marco Rubio insisted Machado's return had been made possible by the US-backed talks — and he urged her to support them.

"We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy," he said.

Huge oil reserves

Last week, thousands demonstrated in Caracas and other cities, demanding Machado's return and elections.

Many leaders from her Vente Venezuela party have recently returned from exile that was prompted by a post-election purge that left 28 dead and resulted in more than 2,400 arrests, including dozens of Machado's associates.

Her party wants elections in 2027 and for her to be allowed to run, unlike the last presidential vote.

title: Brazil rejects Bolsonaro heir to re-elect Lula in closely fought election
text:
In brief Brazil's veteran leader, commonly known as Lula, has held on to power.

A razor-thin election result caps a dramatic political comeback.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, nearly 81, has clinched a fourth term in a tight runoff against Flávio Bolsonaro.

The leftist leader, known as Lula, won 51.7 per cent of the vote, compared to 48.2 per cent for the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, official results showed.

Brazil's election stood at a virtual tie halfway through counting on Monday, with Lula holding a razor-thin lead over the right-wing Bolsonaro.

It was the final electoral battle for Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, pulling off a dramatic turnaround after coming in second to Bolsonaro in the first round of voting.

After a campaign marred by scandal and mudslinging, Monday's vote plunged into chaos when a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours at the request of Lula, who said buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting.

"I've never complained about anything in any election before. Whether I won or lost, I'd just accept it and get ready for the next one. But this time, something abominable is happening," Lula said.

Bolsonaro also requested an extension in some parts of the country due to heavy rains, but his camp lashed out at the country-wide extension.

"It's a disgrace. We've never had anything like this in Brazil, and now they've come up with the idea of extending the election period by two hours. I think it's an attempt to even things out, but Flávio is going to win," Aurelio Junior, a 45-year-old dentist in Brasilia, said.

Jacqueline Maria Lima de Franca, 34, a business owner in Rio de Janeiro backing Lula, said it was "more than fair ... everyone should have the right to vote, and that was being neglected".

'We are watching'

Lula's win cements Brazil as one of Latin America's few leftist nations, refusing to join a regional swing to the right championed by United States President Donald Trump.

Lula, who will now serve a fourth non-consecutive term, pitched himself as a bulwark against US interference and democratic backsliding.

Trump, an ally of Flávio Bolsonaro's father, simply said "we are watching, yeah", when asked about Brazil's election on Sunday.

READ MORE Tens of thousands take to streets in Brazil ahead of closely contested runoff

The 45-year-old Bolsonaro had vowed to crack down on crime and slash government spending, while handing Brazil to "the Lord Jesus Christ".

"The time has come for real change," he declared after voting in Rio de Janeiro.

"This is about renewal, enough of the same old thing," 67-year-old retiree Eduardo Viana told a journalist from the Agence France-Presse news agency, adding that Lula "says he governs for the poor ... just look, people can't even go to the supermarket".

Bolsonaro presented himself as more moderate than his firebrand father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 elections.

After its first-round defeat, the left swung into action with massive rallies highlighting Jair Bolsonaro's chaotic handling of the COVID-19 pandemic, devastation of the Amazon rainforest and cuts to public programs.

Lula's revamp

Lula, revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, made a dramatic comeback to office in the 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months.

The charges, annulled on procedural grounds, have continued to haunt him.

In his third term, he oversaw a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but voters complain about the cost of living and a sense of insecurity.

After his first-round blow, Lula revamped his social media strategy and even bought his first mobile phone.

A fierce social media battle drew in Meta, parent company of WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, which Lula's campaign accused of favouring his opponent with "algorithmic manipulation".

Meta denied this but acknowledged that some of Lula's campaign ads had been mistakenly deactivated due to technical errors.

title: Robodebt recommendations not followed, outcomes 'unfair' under aged care algorithm
text:
IN BRIEF The Commonwealth Ombudsman has highlighted the "serious consequences" of the government's automated assessment tool.

Government staff and health advocates previously raised concerns about inability to override IAT assessments.

A Commonwealth Ombudsman investigation has revealed that the government's aged care tool has led to unfair outcomes and undermined public confidence and safety.

The Department of Health, Disability and Ageing uses a Single Assessment System (SAS) which includes the Integrated Assessment Tool (IAT) introduced on 1 November 2025. The legislatively prescribed tool is used for home care assessments and is automated to determine the level of aged care services an older individual requires.

However, the Ombudsman found that the IAT lacks safeguards and capacity to override incorrect assessments.

"Currently, under the law, automated decisions made by the IAT's algorithm cannot be overridden and changed, even if they are clinically inappropriate," Commonwealth Ombudsman Iain Anderson said on Monday.

"The IAT and its associated decision-making framework do not merely have the potential to undermine public confidence — rather, a reasonable person would, in my view, lack confidence that the system is in fact fair and consistent."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

'Serious consequences'

Around 1.1 million older Australians access aged care services through the home support system.

The SAS has attracted several complaints, particularly about contracted assessment providers using the IAT and its algorithm, the ombudsman said.

Complaints about the SAS detailed poor communication, long wait times, slow review processes, insufficient assessors, and assessors lacking appropriate training and qualifications.

Complaints about the IAT detailed the underassessment of care needs, inability to change automated decisions and limited clinical expertise and algorithmic transparency.

The Ombudsman found no publicly available information on how the IAT determines an outcome — which is "inconsistent with the intentions of the Robodebt Royal Commission recommendations about transparency of government automated decision-making".

Anderson said he believed the department "did not and may still not, understand key components of the legal framework it created".

He said it also did not "understand what legal framework it was meant to create".

The investigation also revealed that the department has been stating assessments automated by IAT could be changed — which is untrue.

"Up until the introduction of the legislation in October 2025, the Department had been incorrectly advising assessment providers and the public that automated IAT outcomes could be changed," he said.

"This had serious consequences."

The Ombudsman also found that the SAS assessment provider performance has been "falling short" of KPIs.

It also found the department has taken a "limited role" in checking training requirements and compliance of assessors using the IAT, and that there are no safeguards protecting the "integrity of the online training".

Prioritise 'meaningful consultation'

The Ombudsman investigation made 10 recommendations to the department, including amending the legislation to allow overrides of automated IAT decisions and conducting a comprehensive review of both the legislation related to the needs assessment process and the business rules underpinning the algorithm.

It also recommended that any changes be "preceded by meaningful consultation with the public" and that the Australian National Audit Office consider a performance audit of the department's use of public resources.

In a statement, Health, Disability and Ageing Minister Mark Butler and Aged Care and Seniors Minister Sam Rae said the government will consider the Ombudsman's report "carefully".

"We’re already acting on many of the recommendations to ensure our aged care system is transparent and reliable, and we’ll examine what further action we can take to give every Australian confidence in the system," they said.

They said the government "accepts or accepts-in-principle all remaining recommendations and will work with other agencies to support responses to recommendations directed outside the portfolio".

In September, The Guardian reported that department staff had warned the Aged Care Minister Sam Rae and Health Minister Mark Butler about removing the IAT's human override function — three days before it was rolled out.

At the time, Motor Neurone Disease Australia CEO Clare Sullivan said the organisations had been "raising serious concerns".

"For months, MND Australia has been raising serious concerns about a system where an algorithm can determine the level of care someone receives without an assessor being able to intervene when the outcome is clearly inappropriate," she said.

"People living with MND do not have the luxury of waiting indefinitely for answers."

READ MORE The 'shadow' tools spreading through government with little scrutiny

She said there needed to be a "clear pathway for experienced assessors to apply clinical judgement when the system gets it wrong".

At the time, the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Ageing and Aged Care Council said it had "consistently raised" that the issues with the IAT were "simply not implementation issues" and rather reflect a "failure in national system design".

"Recognising the failures in the IAT is one thing. The real test is what the government does about it," CEO and Warramunga woman Kim Whiteley said.

"The answer cannot simply be another tool built on the same system assumptions. What comes next must deliver assessments that uphold dignity and respect, are culturally safe and appropriate and genuinely understand the person and their circumstances."

title: 'Lightning in a bottle': The unlikely election issue aligning Trump voters with Democrats
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Just a year ago, few would have predicted what would become one of the surprise political battlegrounds — and unlikely unifiers — in the United States midterm elections.

The explosive growth of gigantic data centres across the country is troubling Republican and Democratic voters alike, creating an unusual point of agreement in an otherwise deeply polarised nation.

But with the data centre boom increasingly concentrated in Republican-leaning or 'red states', Republican officials face a political dilemma. Some are contending with growing opposition to the vast facilities in their communities, even as President Donald Trump vocally advocates for the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

Mike Madrid, a Republican political consultant, tells SBS News: "Rarely have I ever seen an issue like this [that] becomes a social-political movement so rapidly and so intensely."

It's much bigger than the AI data centres. It's the future that they're powering that are causing a lot of angst and concern.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

He says the issue was barely on voters' radar a year or two ago but is now "front row and centre".

Between January and August 2026, the proportion of Republicans who believed data centres negatively affected the quality of life of nearby residents jumped from 24 per cent to 42 per cent, according to a Pew Research Center survey.

Democrats remain more likely to view the facilities negatively, but the shift among Republicans points to a growing source of cross-party discontent.

"I think it has a lot to do with just the rapid pace upon which these things are being approved, particularly in red states," Madrid says.

It could cost a lot of Republicans their congressional districts, their governorships, their Senate seats.

The Stargate AI data center in Abilene, Texas, is part of a $500 billion joint venture to build new infrastructure for companies like OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT. Source: Getty / Bloomberg

In response to the shift in public sentiment, some Republican politicians are backing away from Trump's pro-AI agenda.

Meanwhile, after months of struggling to find a message, Democratic candidates are increasingly seizing on opposition to data centres as a campaign attack line.

As the backlash grows, data centres are becoming an unlikely electoral flashpoint, pitting Trump's AI ambitions against local concerns over energy use, water supplies and the impact on rural communities.

The data centre boom

The US has far more data centres than any other country in the world.

Thirty-eight per cent of Americans now live within about 8km of at least one operational data centre, with more than 3,000 such facilities across the country and another 1,500 in the development pipeline, according to the Pew Research Center.

By comparison, Australia has around 165 operational data centres, and their expansion is already attracting controversy.

Increasingly, it's rural Americans who are finding themselves on the front lines of the data centre boom.

While 87 per cent of existing US data centres are in urban areas, most new developments are now planned for rural areas — where voters are more likely to lean Republican.

Outside Virginia, which has the highest concentration of data centres anywhere in the world, 92 per cent of data centre construction is in states Trump won in 2024, according to an analysis by energy data firm Cleanview Research.

Trump has been an unapologetic champion of data centre expansion, arguing that expanding data centre infrastructure is vital to maintaining US competitiveness in AI. He warned in August that communities that oppose them risk becoming "backwards and poor".

"If we kill the golden goose, you will only have yourselves to blame," he posted on Truth Social at the time.

"China could not be happier with this anti-data centre movement."

Elections analyst Kyle Kondik, managing editor of an election forecasting site run by the University of Virginia Center for Politics, suggests Trump's position on data centres has been at odds with his broader populist approach.

"On this issue, the president has not been populist at all," he tells SBS News.

"So perhaps Democrats have more of an opportunity to bolster their own anti-establishment, populist positioning."

The backlash against data centres

Much of the expansion is being fuelled by the AI boom, which is driving demand for hyperscale data centres.

The number of these large-scale facilities, which typically house thousands of servers that process and store vast amounts of information, has more than quadrupled in the US since 2016, according to Synergy Research Group.

Olivia Shen, director of the Strategic Technologies Program at the United States Studies Centre, says hyperscale facilities differ in scale and resource demands from older data centres that have existed for decades without widespread attention or controversy.

AI models require enormous computing power and electricity, driving demand for ever-larger facilities.

Shen says these developments have caught some rural communities off guard, with residents raising concerns about immense resource consumption, noise, rising energy bills, and a lack of consultation.

"Imagine you've got a small farm you've had for generations, and then suddenly right next door there is this giant black box, but it stretches for kilometres, and it hums all day long with a kind of electricity," she says.

What does that do to your groundwater that you're using for your little farm? What does that mean for your enjoyment of your local environment?

The sheer scale of the developments helps put the concerns into perspective.

The sprawling Switch Citadel data centre campus in Nevada, one of the largest data centre campuses in the US, occupies a site spanning 800 hectares — equivalent to roughly 1,120 football fields.

Virginia, a state roughly one and a half times the size of Tasmania, has more than twice as many operational data centres as the whole of Australia, with more than 450 more planned.

Could data centres turn red voters blue?

Republicans and Democrats in several states have recently adopted tougher rhetoric on data centres or proposed restrictions on new developments.

One of the most prominent reversals is happening in Texas, where Republican governor Greg Abbott has called for sweeping restrictions on data centres. He ordered a temporary pause on approvals for new electricity grid connections in August, before expanding the restrictions the following month.

Less than a year earlier, he had touted Texas as the "epicentre of AI development".

With the 3 November midterm elections approaching, Abbott is facing a tighter-than-expected contest in the longtime red state against Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa — who has dismissed his temporary pause as a "scam" that will end the day after the election.

She has branded data centres the "fight of this election season" and implored Abbott to impose a moratorium on new facilities.

Democrats have invested significantly in attack ads targeting Republican incumbents over data centre development. Source: Getty / Austin American-Statesman/Hearst

Midterm elections typically swing against the party of the sitting president. With Trump's approval rating under pressure amid the soaring cost of living and the war with Iran, Republicans were already facing a challenging electoral environment.

Chris Borick, professor of political science at Pennsylvania's Lehigh University and director of its public opinion research lab, says the data centre debate could be the "new ingredient" that tips the balance against Republican incumbents in multiple closely contested congressional races, including several in Pennsylvania and Ohio.

He says he's studied public opinion for decades, and he's never seen an issue emerge so rapidly as a major concern for voters.

Nothing, in my mind, has an immediate comparison point to how data centres have evolved so quickly as a salient issue for voters across the country.

Protests against data centres, artificial intelligence and Big Tech are popping up across the United States. Source: Getty / Bloomberg

Earlier this month, The Economist published an analysis suggesting that opposition to data centres could even be shifting some of Trump's loyal supporters towards the Democrats.

It found that 17 per cent of people living within 2km of a data centre who voted for Trump in 2024 now say they would support a Democrat, compared with just 6 per cent of Trump voters elsewhere.

"When there are races that are won on razor-thin margins, that shift is significant," Borick tells SBS News.

An unlikely political unifier

Community backlash against data centres also ties into broader anxieties about AI, resource depletion, the potential loss of jobs, wealth disparities and the growing power of Big Tech.

David McCuan, professor of political science at California’s Sonoma State University, tells SBS News: "It does reflect a long-running trend of concerns about what we might broadly call 'quality of life'".

He says Big Tech has joined tobacco, the pharmaceutical industry and oil giants as "one of the big bad boogeymen of American politics".

Those concerns are bringing voters from the opposite ends of the political spectrum into alignment, both locally and nationally, even when their broader political priorities differ.

In one of the most unusual examples, political adversaries Steve Bannon and US senator Bernie Sanders appeared at the same event last month to denounce tech billionaires and call for greater restrictions on AI.

Sanders, a left-wing independent, took the stage immediately after Bannon, a former chief strategist to Trump and a prominent right-wing podcaster, though the two offered different visions for resolving the issue.

Backlash against data centres is the "sole issue that unites both sides of the political spectrum" in this election, McCuan says.

[It] has really grabbed lightning in a bottle.

title: 'Allegations of allegations': Greens senator takes leave amid misconduct investigation

A Greens senator is taking leave from parliament, saying pressure surrounding a misconduct probe has left him "kept out by allegations of allegations".

He has vehemently denied any wrongdoing.

Key points DANCE: The Australian Ballet returns to the State Theatre with The Nutcracker

JAZZ: Melbourne International Jazz festival wraps up for another year

MUSIC: Melbourne Chamber Orchestra performs Twilight Dialogues

MUSIC: Louis Tomlinson puts on a big show at John Cain Arena

DANCE

The Nutcracker ★★★★

The Australian Ballet, Ian Potter State Theatre, Arts Centre Melbourne, until October 31 The State Theatre has reopened after 2½ years of renovations, and Arts Centre Melbourne is keen to reassure audiences that its familiar character survives. The Australian Ballet has taken the hint, returning home with Peter Wright’s The Nutcracker, created for Birmingham Royal Ballet in 1990: an old favourite offering reassurance on a suitably extravagant scale. Yuumi Yamada as Clara in The Nutcracker. Kate Longley John F. Macfarlane’s gigantic, dreamy designs seem almost to have grown out of the theatre. The Stahlbaums’ drawing room, swathed in dark red curtains, extends the auditorium’s crimson plush into the family Christmas party. With festive decorations glistering like seams of emerald in the shadows, the whole experience feels deliciously subterranean: a theatre and a household tucked into the same deep burrow. We’re all here underground together. Yuumi Yamada supplies the youthful enthusiasm this cosy fantasy needs. Her Clara, a ballet student dreaming herself into a ballerina, is eager, unguarded and winsomely adolescent, and her delight in everything has an attractive freedom. Jarryd Madden’s fatherly Drosselmeyer offers a steadying presence.

Advertisement

The finest enchantment in this version remains Wright’s reimagined version of the Dance of the Snowflakes at the end of the first act, led here by Isobelle Dashwood’s graceful Snow Fairy. On Saturday night, the second act sometimes felt rushed. The national dances were briskly dispatched, and the Waltz of the Flowers grew a little unruly, the ensemble’s lines scattering beneath Macfarlane’s overhead tangle of streamers. Intentional or otherwise, the visual rhyme was actually quite enjoyable: the flowers and their consorts seemed to have caught the delirium of the decoration. But the entrance of Sharni Spencer’s queenly Sugar Plum Fairy soon restored order. The battle beneath the Christmas tree impresses. Kate Longley The theatre itself still smells new. The seats are a considerable improvement, although the space between rows feels even more miserly than before. The additional aisles do, however, offer more accessibility. The gridlock in the stalls after the curtain comes down is now, I hope, a thing of the past. The acoustics require a more cautious verdict after one visit, but, still, Orchestra Victoria – led by Jonathan Lo – sounded very good to me, with a notably crisp brass section. Familiarity has its attractions and there is still plenty in this production – such as the battle beneath the Christmas tree – that impresses. On the other hand, after nearly two decades and five seasons in The Australian Ballet’s repertoire, this Nutcracker is starting to feel a little old-fashioned. The building has had its renovation – now for the ballet?

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann

Advertisement

JAZZ

Melbourne International Jazz Festival

Closing weekend, October 23–25 When Tigran Hamasyan was a child, he dreamed of playing guitar in a heavy-metal band. On stage last Friday, he was playing piano in a recital hall rather than shredding on electric guitar for a moshpit full of metalheads, but his incendiary concert left us in no doubt that his childhood ambition was still lodged firmly in his heart and hands. Tigran Hamasyan performs at MIJF Will Hamilton Coates Volume, velocity and virtuosity were the hallmarks of his quartet’s performance on the closing weekend of this year’s Melbourne International Jazz Festival. The delicacy and ethereal beauty that defined Hamasyan’s solo show at the festival in 2017 surfaced occasionally, via hushed melodies and haunting echoes of Armenian folk music. But for every glimpse of light and nuance, there were a hundred frantic runs and pummelling chords, with thundering drums and a bass sound so penetrating that its vibrations were felt more than heard. This was music as extreme sport, the players executing mind-bending rhythmic puzzles and building elaborate, interlocking motifs with astonishing synchronicity as they expanded on the bold vision of Hamasyan’s album Manifeste. Often using his piano as a percussion instrument, Hamasyan pounded the keys with visceral intensity as he sparred with Yessaï Karapetian’s churning keyboards or locked in tight with the jagged momentum of Marc Karapetian’s bass and Arman Mnatsakanyan’s drums.

Advertisement

Witnessing the band at full force felt like riding bareback on a runaway stallion while clinging on for dear life, or being tossed about in a dark, roiling ocean filled with unpredictable currents. It was gripping and immersive, exhilarating and exhausting – a fascinating window into the ever-mutating world of this unique artist. One of the festival’s biggest names, Dee Dee Bridgewater, was scheduled to perform on Saturday, but the US singer withdrew from the festival just days before her concert due to ill health. Losing an international headliner will undoubtedly have left a sizeable dent in the festival’s coffers, but there was still plenty of exceptional music on offer that day. The 10th anniversary of the album Aziza was celebrated as part of this year’s festival. Duncographic The morning drizzle cleared and the clouds parted just in time for Mandisi Dyantyis’ outdoor show in Prahran Square. The South African trumpeter and singer fronted a superb nine-piece local band – Afrospace Interchange – that helped bring Dyantyis’ vibrant music to life. Warm and impassioned, Dyantyis roamed the stage or used gestures to communicate the story of each song, buoyed by the band’s exuberant rhythms, majestic horns and uplifting vocal harmonies. Later that night, American cellist-composer Tomeka Reid and her quartet gave a riveting performance in the newly opened second room at JazzLab – a seriously impressive venue that’s twice the size of the original room while still retaining an air of intimacy.

Advertisement

Drawing on their latest album, dance! skip! hop!, Reid and her remarkable colleagues (guitarist Mary Halvorson, bassist Jason Roebke and drummer Tomas Fujiwara) navigated the leader’s intricate compositions with supreme precision, though the arrangements still left room for spontaneous interplay. This was a highly collaborative affair, with all four instruments given equal prominence. Roles were fluid, too: Reid’s cello could mimic sonorous basslines, pluck deft harmonies or maintain an earthy pulse as her colleagues darted nimbly around her. Her interactions with Halvorson were especially vivid, the pair moving in deft unison or harmony, or conversing in improvised spurts as Halvorson added pitch-bending slides and expressive smears. On Sunday night, bassist and composer Dave Holland – a seminal figure in jazz for more than half a century – took to the stage with three contemporary masters of the genre: saxophonist Chris Potter, guitarist Lionel Loueke and drummer Eric Harland. Reuniting to celebrate the 10th anniversary of their album Aziza, the quartet revisited the repertoire from that album with thrilling vitality. Holland’s agile basslines anchored each piece with effortless authority, underlining the funky swagger of Aziza Dance, the airy calypso shuffle of Summer 15 and the complex metric variations of Blue Sufi. The final number was infused with an upbeat Afro-Latin feel, Loueke trading animated phrases with Potter’s muscular tenor over the rhythm section’s bustling propulsion. The tune? Sleepless Nights – an apt title for patrons who’ve filled their past ten days and nights with memorable music, and a fitting way to farewell this year’s festival.

Reviewed by Jessica Nicholas

MUSIC

Twilight Dialogues ★★★★

Melbourne Chamber Orchestra, 75 Reid St, October 25 Frequent reminders we live in the country with the oldest continuous music practice in the world have hopefully set stale notions about “old world” and “new world” art on their head. The Melbourne Chamber Orchestra performs Twilight Dialogues. Albert Comper This polished and engaging program of clarinet quintets in which Brahms’ beloved work in the genre was preceded by Songs from the Bush written by Melbourne-born pianist and composer Ian Munro, explored subtle connections between European and Australian art music. Dating from 2009, Munro’s three-movement score reveals a masterly grasp of classic chamber music writing, offering intriguing changes of mood and texture. Incorporating folk tunes collected mid last century and an adapted Walmajarri children’s song, he creates a uniquely Australian soundscape.

Advertisement

Country Dance incorporates an unnamed Irish jig while Campfire and Night Sky reimagines classic night music with a freewheeling clarinet over gentle pulsing, muted strings. A Drover’s Lament summons up the pathos of the lonely immigrant before final percussive string effects suggest a ticking clock and the reminiscence of celebrations long ago, whether Indigenous or colonial. David Griffiths’ mellifluous and multi-hued clarinet eloquently voiced the music’s emotional flow, enjoying a fine rapport with the string quartet formed of principals from the Melbourne Chamber Orchestra, especially first violin Sophie Rowell. Together with the other members of the ensemble (violinist Kathryn Taylor, violist Merewyn Bramble and cellist Blair Harris), the Brahms was given a vivid, nuanced performance. The opening tension between restive drama and questing lyricism was well established, while Griffiths excelled in releasing the passionate heartache of the Adagio, muted strings recalling Munro’s use of the same effect. Highly characterised, the sunnier Andantino and the finale’s set of variations demonstrated the players’ tightly knit synergy. Part of the dynamic artistic leadership Rowell brings to the entire MCO enterprise, thought-provoking chamber music concerts such as this are a welcome bonus.

Reviewed by Tony Way

Advertisement

MUSIC

Louis Tomlinson ★★★★

John Cain Arena, October 20 The screams that greet Louis Tomlinson give me a contact high. Die-hard fans have legged it to the barrier and thrust stage. The word “Lemonade” flashes on-screen, towering over Tomlinson and his five-piece band. He cuts an amiable, Gallagher-type figure in a puffy red jacket and jeans. Until he’s briefly engulfed in a confetti explosion. Louis Tomlinson performing at John Cain Arena on October 20. Richard Clifford Music videos are composed live, faces projected dystopia-large with film effects, high-contrast overlays or psychedelic sunflowers, with colour-saturated stage lights and even a synth-laser show for Broken Bones. It’s a leap from the opening act, Rum Jungle, the kind of Aussie indie group you play driving to the beach on P-plates with your mates.

Advertisement

Tomlinson gets somewhat swallowed in the production. The mixing does no favours, his piping, Arctic Monkeys-style vocals no match for thundering drums in songs like The Spark. He’s often lost in backing harmonies and the word-faithful crowd, unless it’s the pared-back cover of the Foo Fighters’ My Hero. But Tomlinson’s impeccable band shines. Oozing rock, they unify eclectic leaps from funk pop and acoustic ballads to nostalgic indie/Britpop like the Oasis-esque Saturdays and Franz Ferdinand-style dance riffs in Out of my System. Keyboard skips between plinking piano and glimmering synth as the guitarists and bassist pace like tigers to tumbling, chest-shaking beats and rip blistering solos. The word “Lemonade” flashes on-screen over Tomlinson and his five-piece band. Richard Clifford Tomlinson performs a pop persona perfectly. Gracious and grateful. Hand on heart, pointing to swooning fans. His grinning, Yorkshire-accented commentary is lightly peppered with profanities: “Loud as you fooken’ can!” In return, the One Direction star is utterly adored. For One Direction’s Night Changes, a sea of phones rise, recording intently. Tomlinson’s grim-faced guards have to pull him back from the barrier when ladies get grabby in the encore. I only wonder if he regretted the jacket in the fervent, feminine body heat filling John Cain Arena.

Red Metal Limited has put another piece of a key metallurgical puzzle in place at its massive Sybella rare earths project near Mount Isa in Queensland, with impressive column leach test results from the Kary Zone’s deeper, more dominant fresh granite ore. The company says two-metre column leach tests on the granite, crushed to 10 millimetres, achieved solid neodymium and praseodymium recoveries of 65 per cent and 68 per cent, respectively. Notably, the result was achieved with a total acid consumption of just 19 kilograms per tonne of sulphuric acid at ambient temperature, which is materially lower than the 23–27kg used in tests for the two other weathered ore types that sit above it. Surface granite (pictured) at Red Metal Limited’s Sybella project sitting just 20km from the major mining hub of Mount Isa in Queensland. Neodymium and praseodymium are particularly valuable because they are used to manufacture powerful permanent magnets for electric vehicles, wind turbines and industrial equipment. In heap leaching, a chemical solution is trickled through the crushed ore to dissolve the valuable metals, which are then collected from the liquid and recovered. Low acid consumption is important because acid can be one of the biggest costs in heap leaching.

Advertisement

‘The new data will feed into our current Sybella PFS to assess the potential economics of this very large rare earth project.’ Red Metal Limited managing director Rob Rutherford The fresh granite accounts for the lion’s share of the Kary Zone’s monster 936-million-tonne (Mt) inferred mineral resource, weighing in at 598Mt, while the overlying saprock and transitional ores contribute 182Mt and 157Mt respectively. With all three ore types now successfully tested, the company appears to have cleared a major hurdle on its path to a prefeasibility study (PFS). The Kary Zone resource currently grades 334 parts per million (ppm) neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) and 31.7ppm dysprosium-terbium (DyTb) at a 300ppm NdPr cut-off. Intriguingly, the mineralisation remains open at depth, with drilling encountering rare earths down to 240 metres, suggesting the deposit could potentially become bigger with further drilling. Meanwhile, the company is running a separate test using 20mm crushed ore packed into 150mm-diameter columns standing six metres tall to closely replicate the conditions of a commercial heap leach pad. The final results are expected to build on Red Metal’s previously successful two-metre column program, which delivered impressive neodymium recoveries of 76 per cent from transitional ore and 71 per cent from saprock. Praseodymium recoveries were equally encouraging, reaching 78 per cent and 72 per cent from the respective ore types. Red Metal Limited managing director Rob Rutherford said: “The positive column leach test on the fresh granite mineralisation from the Kary Zone has demonstrated the heap leach potential of the very large fresh granite resource located immediately below the near-surface, saprock and transitional ores which remains open at depth.”

Advertisement

In parallel with its metallurgical work, the company has drill rods already turning on a 5000-metre campaign aiming to both upgrade and extend the Kary Zone deposit. Infill drilling is targeting near-surface, rich zones, while extensional drilling is testing the interpreted southeast extension where previous work hinted at higher-grade potential. Management describes the Sybella deposit as geologically unique, with abundant granite-hosted soft ore, giving the project a compelling edge and offering simple crushing and processing options. Sybella lies in a 12km long by 3km wide granite-pervasive corridor and holds an enormous global resource of 4.795 billion tonnes grading 302ppm NdPr. These metals sit alongside the more valuable heavy rare earths dysprosium and terbium at a combined 28ppm, with yttrium adding a further 136ppm. The results have landed at an opportune time, as Australia and its allies ramp up efforts to loosen China’s grip on global rare earths supply chains, with government-backed financing and strategic-reserve measures increasingly focused on the critical minerals sector. Against that backdrop, a large, shallow, granite-hosted resource that has demonstrated ambient-temperature heap-leach potential - and includes both light and heavy magnet rare earths - is likely to attract attention. While Sybella is the clear flagship, Red Metal is also pursuing a “Big Copper” strategy in the famed Mt Isa province, hunting for giant iron-oxide-copper-gold discoveries similar to the nearby Ernest Henry and Osborne deposits. The company recently expanded its footprint in the region, lodging 17 new tenement applications near its Gulf and Three Ways projects to bring its total landholding to a vast 5800 square kilometres.

Advertisement

The company is also running a high-resolution airborne gravity survey at Mt Isa, piggybacking on concurrent regional airborne gravity surveys conducted by the Geological Survey of Queensland and Geoscience Australia. With metallurgical work de-risking its processing pathway, drills turning to expand its already giant resource and a separate hunt for monster copper deposits underway, Red Metal looks to be firing on all cylinders. The completion of the Sybella PFS, slated for the first quarter of 2027 and results from the six-metre column test will likely be the next key catalysts as the company sketches out the economics of its potentially world-class asset. Dean Solomon to join Damien Hardwick at Gold Coast Melbourne captain Max Gawn has applauded the club’s “brutal” list-management calls which led to the departure of favourite son Jack Viney, but hopes he can finish his career as a one-club player. Gawn is off contract in 2027, but at 33 is still playing some of the best football of his career, which he attributes, in part, to his punishing off-season cycling regime. Melbourne captain Max Gawn cycles alongside Tour de France champion Cadel Evans ahead of the Great Ocean Road race. AAPIMAGE The 2021 premiership skipper won All-Australian selection for the ninth time in 2026, and is keen to remain a Demon for life when contract discussions open. However, he understands the business of football, having watched his fellow premiership on-ball brigade of Clayton Oliver, Christian Petracca and Viney, along with key defender Steven May, depart over the past two seasons.

“I’m pretty keen in Melbourne. I understand ‘Vines’ would have said the same thing 12 months ago. So, I’ve just applauded ‘Lamby’ [list boss Tim Lamb] and King [coach Steven King], and if I’m the one that has to move on next year, and I still think there’s footy ahead of me, then that conversation will come, but right now, it does look like my finish will be with the Demons,” Gawn said on Monday. However, speaking as an ambassador at the launch of the Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race, Gawn hinted he would be open to offers, should negotiations with the Demons not go as planned, and if new club Tasmania came calling. Kicking on: Melbourne skipper Max Gawn is off contract in 2027, and wants to finish his career as a one-club player. So if SBS want to jump into my phone … but, no, I’m pretty keen to finish up in Melbourne.”

Gawn said he was delighted that Essendon and the Eagles showed interest in Viney, his former co-captain. “I went from a little bit of surprise [at his departure], and then I went a little bit of other clubs were making him feel generally loved,” Gawn said. Fresh start: Ex-Melbourne midfielder Jack Viney will continue his career with West Coast after being traded to the Eagles on the final day of the trade period. So I’m really excited for him.” Gawn said the Demons had needed a substantial make-over, having seen how quickly Geelong transformed, even after winning the 2022 premiership. Only nine Demons players now remain from the 2021 premiership team.

“I sat there and looked at that [2022 Geelong] team, I was like, OK, and then they play in the grand final three years later, and they had 10 or 15 new players in that team. And, at the same time, Melbourne was still running the round with the ’21 premiership team,” Gawn said. It’s like, OK, this is what’s needed in a way to stay in the modern game.” A cycling enthusiast who now has his own podcast on the sport, Gawn’s pre-season training program has so far included “Everesting” South Australia’s exhausting Willunga Hill, riding the 3.7km climb 39.5 times in 21 hours, and another punishing ride on the island of Phuket in Thailand. Gather Round games revealed The AFL has scheduled three blockbuster games at the Adelaide Oval to underpin Gather Round, giving fans the first glimpse of its 2027 fixture on Monday. Round four will open on Thursday April 8, with the Crows seeking revenge for their semi-final loss in 2026 to the Brisbane Lions, and close four days later with Western Bulldogs gun recruit Zak Butters facing his former side Port Adelaide for the first time. In between, the league has scheduled a humdinger of a Saturday-night match between leading premiership fancies Fremantle and Hawthorn.

There are two other games scheduled at the Adelaide Oval across the weekend – Sydney v Collingwood on the Friday night and an early Saturday game between Carlton and Melbourne, who met in a wildcard final in 2026. Gold Coast, GWS, Geelong and St Kilda are the four teams heading to the Barossa for their Gather Round games, while Richmond, West Coast, Essendon and North Melbourne are bound for Norwood Oval. Look away, Port fans: Zak Butters in Western Bulldogs colours. Getty Images South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas – an avid Power fan – was quick to spruik the Gather Round program, which coincides with the Easter school holidays, and the inclusion of a players’ parade on the Friday. “The blockbuster weekend of footy will be boosted with the inaugural Players Parade on Friday, allowing fans to see their heroes from all 18 clubs in one spot,” he said. “Personally, I’m looking forward to being at a packed Adelaide Oval to see Zak Butters take on his former teammates.”

Solomon gets Gold Coast gig After coaching Essendon through the second half of 2026, Dean Solomon will return to Gold Coast as an assistant coach to Damien Hardwick. Dean Solomon as coach of Essendon. Getty Images Solomon, now 46, was on the coaching staff at the Suns from the club’s inception in the AFL in 2011 to 2020, even serving three games as interim coach following the departure of Rodney Eade in 2017. Solomon later joined the board at Essendon – the club where he made his name as a player and was part of the 2000 premiership team – but relinquished that position a year ago to return to a hands-on coaching role.

Advertisement

He started the 2026 season as an assistant to Brad Scott, and became the club’s stop-gap coach when Scott was sacked mid-season. Despite holding some ambition to become the senior coach permanently, Solomon’s hopes were dented by a record of just one win from his 12 games in charge. After hiring Solomon’s former teammate Mark McVeigh as senior coach for 2027, Essendon announced last month that Solomon had declined their offer of another role in the football department and would return to live in NSW with his wife and children. On Monday, the Suns spruiked Solomon’s recruitment as a homecoming. “Dean played a significant role across our club’s first decade in the competition, and his expertise and industry experience will be instrumental in helping us take steps forward in the years ahead,” Gold Coast’s general manager of football Craig Cameron said. Solomon said the Suns job aligned with his family circumstances .

Billionaire James Packer has paid at least $US1.25 million ($1.78 million) to the Tel Aviv law firm also defending Benjamin Netanyahu against allegations the Israeli prime minister corruptly received benefits from the Australian businessman and other wealthy supporters a decade ago. An investigation by this masthead on the eve of seismic Israeli elections has uncovered a money trail involving monthly $US50,000 wire transfers over the past two years from a bank account controlled by Packer’s company to the account of Netanyahu’s legal defence firm. Australian businessman James Packer (left) and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Aresna Villanueva The first monthly “retainer” payment from the Citibank account of Packer’s firm Consolidated Press International was made on September 23, 2024 to the account of law firm Hadad Roth Shenhar at Israel’s Mizrahi Tefahot bank. The monthly payments, which Packer has not denied, have continued for two years. A source aware of the payments, but not authorised to speak publicly, said they should be urgently investigated to determine if Netanyahu was receiving an undisclosed benefit from Packer as the law firm defends the Israeli prime minister over allegations he unlawfully accepted expensive gifts from Packer between 2014 and 2016.

Advertisement

Israeli authorities have repeatedly blocked Netanyahu from receiving funds from wealthy backers to pay for his defence in his long-running corruption case. This masthead has not confirmed that Netanyahu benefited from the payments. Editor's pick Courts Star chefs, cigars and pink champagne: How James Packer made a mark in Israel If it was found Packer’s payments to the law firm directly or indirectly benefited Netanyahu, the source alleged the payments could involve fresh breaches of Israeli laws governing how politicians can accept support, and might also fall under US laws that govern financial transactions or possible benefits foreign politicians receive from businesses. Asked about the allegations on Monday morning, a spokesperson for Netanyahu said: “I couldn’t give a monkey’s about your questions. “We are very busy. We have an election on right now.”

Advertisement

When contacted by this masthead on Friday night, Packer did not deny the rolling $US50,000 payments but declined to comment. A source familiar with the 59-year-old former media mogul’s financial dealings later insisted the wire transfers to Netanyahu’s lawyers were for work done for Packer – including “deal finding” in Israel where Packer has business interests – and unrelated to the prime minister’s court case. Netanyahu (left) and Packer (right) at the United Nations in 2016. Ten News This masthead subsequently requested evidence of any deals in Israel or work undertaken by the law firm, but neither Packer nor his company have yet responded. In addition to running Netanyahu’s defence against claims the Israeli leader broke his country’s law by accepting luxury goods from Packer and wealthy film producer Arnon Milchan, law firm Hadad Roth Shenhar is helping Netanyahu contest allegations that he improperly traded favours with an Israeli newspaper publisher and telecommunications company.

Advertisement

Netanyahu’s primary defence attorney is Hadad Roth Shenhar’s most senior lawyer, Amit Hadad. Hadad has gained prominence by appearing for several Israeli government ministers and business identities, but Netanyahu is his most notable client. Netanyahu in 2024 with lawyer Amit Hadad (right). AP Hadad did not respond to questions from this masthead. In addition to the ongoing corruption trial, Netanyahu has controversially, and unsuccessfully, sought legal permission allowing his wealthy overseas friends to fund the law firm Hadad Roth Shenhar. Israeli authorities have ruled Netanyahu cannot rely on the rich backers because this would amount to a breach of trust and conflict of interest.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Updated

Courts Netanyahu assails media as he testifies for first time in his corruption trial Transparency International said Packer’s decision to pay $US1.25 million to the law firm defending Netanyahu demanded urgent and independent scrutiny. “As there are already significant corruption charges against Mr Netanyahu relating to past gifts from Mr Packer, and other business associates, these new allegations must be thoroughly investigated by authorities,” said Transparency International’s Australian director, Clancy Moore. Moore also cautioned that evidence might yet show the payments were unrelated to Netanyahu. Moore stressed scrutiny was also required in light of the previous concerns about who could pay for Netanyahu’s legal fees. “Significantly, Israeli authorities have repeatedly ruled that Mr Netanyahu can’t use funds from foreign benefactors to fund his legal defence against corruption charges due to conflict of interests and his failure to disclose his wealth,” Moore said.

Advertisement

Packer found himself entangled in Netanyahu’s corruption case after gifting the prime minister champagne and cigars more than a decade ago, but has not been accused of any wrongdoing and has not been called as a witness to the prime minister’s corruption trial. An aerial view of the beachside villas Benjamin Netanyahu (left in circle) and James Packer owned in the gated community on Hadar Street, in Caesarea, about 45 minutes north of Tel Aviv, Israel. Google Maps Packer and Netanyahu at the time lived in neighbouring villas in the exclusive township of Caesarea and were regular guests at each other’s homes. Netanyahu even had a key to Packer’s luxury property. Packer once called the Israeli prime minister “probably the most impressive man I’ve ever met”. Australian Federal Police officers interviewed Packer on behalf of their Israeli counterparts in late 2017 but stressed he was a witness in the case – not a suspect – and that he co-operated fully.

Advertisement

Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict October 7 changed their lives. Now they are running for office This masthead submitted detailed questions to Packer’s privately owned Consolidated Press Holdings (CPH). The company did not reply. The questions included whether it was appropriate for Packer to make payments to Netanyahu’s law firm given it was defending him in a case which involved the Australian businessman, and why Hadad Roth Shenhar was selected for investment advice. Consolidated Press International (CPI) is one of several private investment arms operated by Packer. At the time that payments to Netanyahu’s law firm began, CPI had more than $600 million in investments in technology companies including Taiwan semiconductor Nvidia and Facebook owner Meta. Packer later pivoted to gambling stocks through large stakes in Las Vegas-based poker machine manufacturer Light and Wonder, and Sportsbet’s parent company Flutter. He has also invested heavily in AI.

Advertisement

Tuesday’s election in Israel represents a crucial juncture for the Middle East, with Netanyahu’s right-wing government facing potential defeat. His removal from office would trigger a reset of the conflicts in Iran and Gaza and redraw the relationship between Jerusalem and US President Donald Trump. Packer and film producer Arnon Milchan (centre) listen to Netanyahu speak at a joint meeting of the US Congress in 2015. Getty Netanyahu – Israel’s longest serving prime minister and the country’s first sitting leader to be charged with a crime – has repeatedly invoked the security situation in the Middle East to argue for delays in giving evidence at his corruption trial. Known as Case 1000, Netanyahu was in 2019 indicted on fraud and breach of trust charges for accepting luxury gifts from Packer and film producer Arnon Milchan worth about $295,000. Netanyahu is also accused of intervening on behalf of Milchan for various business matters, including a US visa renewal. The 77-year-old prime minister completed his evidence on these charges and other unrelated allegations in July. The court is yet to deliver a verdict.

Advertisement

Related Article Israel Israel’s Netanyahu seeks a pardon to end his long-running corruption trial. Will he get one? Milchan gave evidence via video link 2023, and told the heavily fortified courtroom in Tel Aviv: “I know that Packer really wanted to be connected and endear himself to Netanyahu.” The Israeli leader and Packer became estranged after the corruption allegations first emerged in 2016 and did not talk for up to eight years. However, the pair reconnected around the time Netanyahu addressed US Congress in July 2024, when Packer sat in the viewing gallery as a special guest. They later shared a Shabbat dinner. The first payment by Packer to the PM’s law firm was made eight weeks after the two rekindled their friendship The prime minister earlier this year asked Israeli President Isaac Herzog to be pardoned to end the long-running legal saga, claiming the trial was “undermining national unity”, and that a pardon would help Israel “tap new opportunities with the US”.

As the new airport opens in western Sydney, we take a look at how it became a reality. See all stories .

The first international commercial flight has flown from Western Sydney International to Auckland, New Zealand. Air New Zealand flight NZ166 took off at 9.17am, the first international departure from the airport, before landing two hours and 41 minutes later in Auckland at 1.58pm local time. WSI’s first domestic flight – a Jetstar flight to the Gold Coast – took place yesterday. The plane had touched down earlier on Monday at Western Sydney International (WSI), arriving from Auckland at 7.27am. The trans-Tasman flight marks the start of the airline’s travel to WSI, where it will fly three times weekly from Auckland. Matt and Serena Ross are among the passengers on the flight to Auckland. Chris Zappone NZ166 passengers Matt and Serena Ross said they were pleased with the option of a second airport in Sydney.

Advertisement

“It’s a milestone event, so it’s special to be part of that,” said Serena. “Having more options for Kiwi travellers to come here will be great.” Related Article Western Sydney International ‘Final piece of the puzzle’: Western Sydney Airport opens for business “It’s nice to see a flash new airport up and running,” said Matt, but added the opening of WSI came as “a bit of surprise”. The couple took a long Uber ride to arrive at WSI. They had assumed when they booked their tickets they would be leaving from Kingsford-Smith Airport at Mascot. “Glad we checked our tickets to verify what airport they were flying out of,” he said. In keeping with the Air New Zealand brand, the flight featured headrest coverings emblazoned with the words “First Flight Feels”.

Advertisement

The flight had 164 passengers and a cabin crew of five, one more than usual for the occasion. It began with a reception for passengers that included snacks and a bevy of camera crews snapping pictures and filming the event. Speaking aboard the WSI-Auckland flight, passengers Denis and Monica said they live “five minutes away” from the airport and had been hearing about its construction for 40 years. The couple said they were “excited” about the prospects of a new airport that will act as a gateway for international travel. Loading “We’ll be flying all around the world,” said Denis. At the same time, Monica said cargo flights near their home were a source of late-night noise. “You do hear a loud noise on the large planes. It sounds like a bit of a rumble, but it’s [a matter of] getting used to it,” said Monica.

Advertisement

Air New Zealand will fly three times weekly to Auckland, serving the existing community and business ties between western Sydney and New Zealand. It will be followed by Singapore Airlines in November, and Fiji Airways and Qatar Airways next year. Air New Zealand chief operations officer Kate Boyer said in “western Sydney for us there’s a huge Kiwi population here, a big expat community, so there are friends and family connections.” “There’s business and trade links, there’s cargo, so it’s a fantastic destination.” Air New Zealand has probably the strongest Pacific destination network in the world, Boyer said with “huge connections into all of the Pacific islands that we serve”.

Advertisement

In opening flights to WSI, the airline expects to be “able to connect people back to their family in New Zealand or the broader Pacific region”. It may also give its planes a bigger slice of the trans-Tasman travel. The federal government hopes the curfew-free airport will offer more flexibility for international carriers that helps bring more business and visitors and allows for more flexibility for Australians going abroad. While Sydney’s time difference with New Zealand is only two hours, coordinating connections for long-haul flights to more distant hubs in Asia or the Middle East can be difficult from Australian airports where curfews apply. The ability to take off and land 24 hours a day will aid long-haul carriers serving Australia. Trans-Tasman corporate bookings are on the rise, increasing 8.4 per cent year-on-year, according to Flight Centre data.

Advertisement

Flight capacity across all carriers on the Australia-New Zealand route is also on track to grow through the rest of the year, Flight Centre said, with seat numbers rising 7 and 8 per cent year-on-year in the final three months of the year. Air New Zealand’s flight will give the western Sydney business community “direct access to New Zealand for the first time,” said Renos Rologas, ANZ general manager of FCM Travel, Flight Centre Travel Group’s corporate travel outfit. “It’s also a fitting backdrop for this quarter’s booking growth, led by construction, manufacturing, and healthcare and social assistance – sectors with people and projects on the ground on both sides of the Tasman.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
